The instruction not to let it touch water in 13:1 means it is never washed, so it takes the shape and stain of the man wearing it, which is the whole force of the sign in 13:11.

The same Hebrew word used for the Euphrates, which is why some English versions read Euphrates here. There is also a place called Parah in Benjamin, listed in Joshua 18:23, a few miles from Jeremiah's home town, which would make the round trip in 13:4-7 walkable rather than a pair of journeys of some seven hundred miles. The text gives the name without explaining it.

The word in 13:12 covers both a large pottery jar and a whole animal skin sewn shut and used as a wine container. The saying sounds like an idiot's remark, every jar gets filled with wine, and the people say so. The reply in 13:13 takes the obvious line and turns it: God is the one doing the filling, and what He fills them with is drunkenness.

translationNotes.term: Can the Cushite change his skin
translationNotes.note: A Cushite is a person from Cush, the kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan and southern Egypt. Cushites served in Judah's court and army, and Ebed-melech in 38:7-13 is one. Verse 23 uses two things that do not change, a man's skin and a leopard's spots, as a proverb about settled habit. It is a statement about fixedness, not about worth.

The king's mother held a formal position at the Judean court with her own throne, seen in 1 Kings 2:19 and 15:13. That is why 13:18 addresses two people and tells both to come down. In 2 Kings 24:12 and 24:15 Jehoiachin's mother Nehushta is deported alongside him by name.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Jeremiah to bury a linen belt, then retrieve it ruined to symbolize how Judah will be destroyed for rejecting him; he warns that all the land will be filled with drunkenness and exile, with no escape for those who have forgotten God and worshiped false gods.

stories.title: 🌵 Jeremiah 14
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought: (14:1).
“Judah mourns and her gates languish. Her people wail for the land, and a cry goes up from Jerusalem. (14:2).
The nobles send their servants for water; they go to the cisterns, but find no water; their jars return empty. They are ashamed and humiliated; they cover their heads. (14:3).
The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen on the land. The farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads. (14:4).
Even the doe in the field deserts her newborn fawn because there is no grass. (14:5).
Wild donkeys stand on barren heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail for lack of pasture.” (14:6).
Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name. Indeed, our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You. (14:7).
O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress, why are You like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who stays but a night? (14:8).
Why are You like a man taken by surprise, like a warrior powerless to save? Yet You are among us, O LORD, and we are called by Your name. Do not forsake us! (14:9).

This is what the LORD says about this people: “Truly they love to wander; they have not restrained their feet. So the LORD does not accept them; He will now remember their iniquity and punish them for their sins.” (14:10).
Then the LORD said to me, “Do not pray for the well-being of this people. (14:11).

Although they may fast, I will not listen to their cry; although they may offer burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them. Instead, I will finish them off by sword and famine and plague.” (14:12).
“Ah, Lord GOD!” I replied, “Look, the prophets are telling them, ‘You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place.’” (14:13).

“The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,” replied the LORD. “I did not send them or appoint them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a false vision, a worthless divination, the futility and delusion of their own minds. (14:14).

Therefore this is what the LORD says about the prophets who prophesy in My name: I did not send them, yet they say, ‘No sword or famine will touch this land.’ By sword and famine these very prophets will meet their end! (14:15).

And the people to whom they prophesy will be thrown into the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword. There will be no one to bury them or their wives, their sons or their daughters. I will pour out their own evil upon them. (14:16).

You are to speak this word to them: ‘My eyes overflow with tears; day and night they do not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people has been shattered by a crushing blow, a severely grievous wound. (14:17).
If I go out to the country, I see those slain by the sword; if I enter the city, I see those ravaged by famine! For both prophet and priest travel to a land they do not know.’” (14:18).

Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion? Why have You stricken us so that we are beyond healing? We hoped for peace, but no good has come, and for the time of healing, but there was only terror. (14:19).
We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers; indeed, we have sinned against You. (14:20).
For the sake of Your name do not despise us; do not disgrace Your glorious throne. Remember Your covenant with us; do not break it. (14:21).
Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? Is this not by You, O LORD our God? So we put our hope in You, for You have done all these things. (14:22).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 28:23-24: The sky like bronze and the ground like iron, with rain turned to dust, in the covenant curses.
Leviticus 26:18-20: Heaven made like iron and strength spent for nothing when the people will not listen.
1 Kings 17:1: Elijah announces years without dew or rain, the same discipline this drought applies.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22: The test of a prophet, and the death penalty for speaking in the LORD's name what He never commanded.
Exodus 32:11-14: Moses pleads for Israel and God relents, the intercession Jeremiah is forbidden to repeat in 14:11.

translationNotes.note: Verse 3 sends servants to the pits and they come back with empty vessels and covered heads. Judah had almost no year-round rivers; households and towns lived off winter rain caught in plastered rock cisterns. A failed rainy season did not mean rationing, it meant the tanks ran dry and there was no other source, which is why 14:4 says the ground is cracked and the farmers cover their heads.

translationNotes.term: The hind and the wild donkeys
translationNotes.note: Verses 5-6 pick two animals a Judean knew as tough survivors. The doe abandons her newborn fawn because there is nothing green, and the wild donkeys stand on the bare heights panting like jackals with their eyes failing. The drought is measured by what it does to creatures that normally need no help.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרֶב רָעָב וְדֶבֶר (herev, ra'av, we-dever)
translationNotes.note: A fixed trio used more than a dozen times in Jeremiah, at 14:12, 21:9, 24:10, 27:8, 32:24, 38:2, 42:17 and elsewhere. They are the three linked killers of an ancient siege in sequence: the army outside, the food running out inside, and disease spreading through a crowded city with no way to bury its dead.

Verse 8 draws on the duty of hospitality. A traveller in the ancient Near East had a claim on shelter for the night and moved on in the morning with no further obligation. The complaint is that God is behaving like a guest with no stake in the household, in a land He had called His own.

stories.keyTakeaway: A severe drought afflicts Judah, prompting Jeremiah to intercede for the people, but the LORD forbids his prayer and declares he will destroy them with sword, famine, and plague. The LORD also condemns the false prophets who are lying in his name and promising peace, saying they and the people will perish.

stories.title: 🌵 Jeremiah 15
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to me: “Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people. Send them from My presence, and let them go! (15:1).

If they ask you, ‘Where shall we go?’ you are to tell them that this is what the LORD says: ‘Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.’ (15:2).
I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to drag away, and the birds of the air and beasts of the earth to devour and destroy. (15:3).
I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem. (15:4).
Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Who will mourn for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? (15:5).
You have forsaken Me, declares the LORD. You have turned your back. So I will stretch out My hand against you and I will destroy you; I am weary of showing compassion. (15:6).
I will scatter them with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land. I will bereave and destroy My people who have not turned from their ways. (15:7).
I will make their widows more numerous than the sand of the sea. I will bring a destroyer at noon against the mothers of young men. I will suddenly bring upon them anguish and dismay. (15:8).

The mother of seven will grow faint; she will breathe her last breath. Her sun will set while it is still day; she will be disgraced and humiliated. And the rest I will put to the sword in the presence of their enemies,” declares the LORD. (15:9).
Woe to me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife and conflict in all the land. I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me. (15:10).
The LORD said: “Surely I will deliver you for a good purpose; surely I will intercede with your enemy in your time of trouble, in your time of distress. (15:11).
Can anyone smash iron — iron from the north — or bronze? (15:12).
Your wealth and your treasures I will give up as plunder, without charge for all your sins within all your borders. (15:13).
Then I will enslave you to your enemies in a land you do not know, for My anger will kindle a fire that will burn against you.” (15:14).
You understand, O LORD; remember me and attend to me. Avenge me against my persecutors. In Your patience, do not take me away. Know that I endure reproach for Your honor. (15:15).
Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart’s delight. For I bear Your name, O LORD God of Hosts. (15:16).
I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them. Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone, for You have filled me with indignation. (15:17).
Why is my pain unending, and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? You have indeed become like a mirage to me— water that is not there. (15:18).

Therefore this is what the LORD says: “If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence. And if you speak words that are noble instead of worthless, you will be My spokesman. It is they who must turn to you, but you must not turn to them. (15:19).
Then I will make you a wall to this people, a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you but will not overcome you, for I am with you to save and deliver you, declares the LORD. (15:20).
I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless.” (15:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:11-14: Moses stands between God and Israel and turns the wrath away, the first precedent named in 15:1.
1 Samuel 7:8-9: Samuel cries to the LORD for Israel and is answered, the second precedent named in 15:1.
2 Kings 21:10-16: Manasseh's sins given as the reason Judah will be wiped clean, which 15:4 cites by name.
Ezekiel 3:8-9: God makes a prophet's forehead hard as flint against a stubborn people, matching the bronze wall of 15:20.
Job 3:1-3: Job curses the day of his birth, the same cry Jeremiah raises in 15:10.

translationNotes.note: Verse 3 appoints four in order: the sword to kill, the dogs to drag, the birds and the beasts to devour. Each stage is the loss of a burial. Judeans expected to be laid in a family tomb, so a body left in the open for scavengers was the final disgrace, and 22:19 uses the same idea against Jehoiakim.

King of Judah for fifty-five years in the first half of the seventh century BC, the longest reign in Judah's history. 2 Kings 21 records him rebuilding the shrines Hezekiah pulled down, putting altars in the temple courts, burning his own son, practising divination, and filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. Verse 4 names him as the reason the sentence stands even after Josiah's reforms.

A wooden fork used on the threshing floor to toss beaten grain into the evening breeze so the chaff blows off and the heavy kernels drop back. Verse 7 says God will winnow them at the gates of the land: the tool is ordinary farm work, and the image is a nation thrown into the wind.

translationNotes.term: Can iron be broken, iron from the north
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 asks whether ordinary iron can break northern iron and bronze. Iron worked with added carbon and quenched is far harder than plain wrought iron, and the northern trade supplied the better metal. The question is a smith's question, and the answer is no.

Verse 18 accuses God of being like a wadi. A wadi is a dry streambed that runs hard in the winter rains and is bone dry by summer, exactly when a traveller needs it. It is the strongest complaint in the book, and 15:19 answers it with a condition rather than a rebuke.

stories.keyTakeaway: God declares he will send destruction on Judah through sword, famine, and captivity because they have rejected him, while Jeremiah laments his suffering and God promises to restore and protect him if he repents and speaks God's words faithfully.

stories.title: 🚫 Jeremiah 16
summaryBullets: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, (16:1).
“You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place.” (16:2).
For this is what the LORD says concerning the sons and daughters born in this place, and the mothers who bore them, and the fathers who fathered them in this land: (16:3).

“They will die from deadly diseases. They will not be mourned or buried, but will lie like dung on the ground. They will be finished off by sword and famine, and their corpses will become food for the birds of the air and beasts of the earth.” (16:4).

Indeed, this is what the LORD says: “Do not enter a house where there is a funeral meal. Do not go to mourn or show sympathy, for I have removed from this people My peace, My loving devotion, and My compassion,” declares the LORD. (16:5).
“Both great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried or mourned, nor will anyone cut himself or shave his head for them. (16:6).
No food will be offered to comfort those who mourn the dead; not even a cup of consolation will be given for the loss of a father or mother. (16:7).
You must not enter a house where there is feasting and sit down with them to eat and drink. (16:8).

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am going to remove from this place, before your very eyes and in your days, the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom. (16:9).

When you tell these people all these things, they will ask you, ‘Why has the LORD pronounced all this great disaster against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?’ (16:10).

Then you are to answer them: ‘It is because your fathers have forsaken Me, declares the LORD, and followed other gods, and served and worshiped them. They abandoned Me and did not keep My instruction. (16:11).
And you have done more evil than your fathers. See how each of you follows the stubbornness of his evil heart instead of obeying Me. (16:12).
So I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known. There you will serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.’ (16:13).
Yet behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they will no longer say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.’ (16:14).

Instead they will say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.’ For I will return them to their land that I gave to their forefathers. (16:15).

But for now I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them. After that I will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them down on every mountain and hill, even from the clefts of the rocks. (16:16).
For My eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from My face, and their guilt is not concealed from My eyes. (16:17).

And I will first repay them double their iniquity and their sin, because they have defiled My land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and they have filled My inheritance with their abominations.” (16:18).

O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress, the nations will come to You from the ends of the earth, and they will say, “Our fathers inherited nothing but lies, worthless idols of no benefit at all. (16:19).
Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods!” (16:20).
“Therefore behold, I will inform them, and this time I will make them know My power and My might; then they will know that My name is the LORD. (16:21).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 24:15-24: Ezekiel is likewise forbidden to mourn his wife, and his silence is made a sign to the people.
Deuteronomy 14:1: The law against gashing yourself or shaving the front of your head for the dead, the customs named in 16:6.
Jeremiah 22:18-19: The funeral rites withheld in 16:4-6, denied to Jehoiakim by name.
Jeremiah 23:7-8: The same saying about a new oath, sworn no longer by the exodus from Egypt but by the return from the north.
Deuteronomy 30:3-5: God gathers His people from the farthest place and brings them back to the land.

translationNotes.note: A funeral gathering with a communal meal and drinking, held for the bereaved household. Neighbours brought food and shared the cup of consolation named in 16:7, because a house in mourning did not cook for itself. Forbidding Jeremiah to attend cuts him out of the ordinary social duties of his own town.

translationNotes.term: Gashing and shaving for the dead
translationNotes.note: Mourners cut their skin and shaved the head or the beard, practices Leviticus 19:28 and Deuteronomy 14:1 forbid to Israel and which 16:6 reports were being done anyway. The point of 16:6-7 is not approval; it is that the coming deaths will be so many that even the customary rites, lawful or not, will stop entirely.

Two methods of taking, in order. Fishermen dragged a net and took everything in the water at once. Hunters worked the rocks and clefts afterward for whatever escaped the net. Verse 16 puts them in sequence to say the sweep will be followed by a search.

Marriage and children were the normal expectation for an Israelite man, and childlessness was counted a loss, so the order in 16:2 is a public act. It is given with a reason attached in 16:3-4: the children born in that place are going to die of disease and sword and lie unburied, so Jeremiah is being kept from producing them.

stories.keyTakeaway: God forbids Jeremiah to marry and commands him to avoid funeral meals and celebrations, signaling the coming judgment where people will die unburied and unmourned because they abandoned God for idols and followed evil more wickedly than their ancestors. God promises future restoration but will first hunt down the people and repay them double for their wickedness and idolatry.

stories.title: 🚫 Jeremiah 17
summaryBullets: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars. (17:1).
Even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills. (17:2).
O My mountain in the countryside, I will give over your wealth and all your treasures as plunder, because of the sin of your high places, within all your borders. (17:3).
And you yourself will relinquish the inheritance that I gave you. I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know, for you have kindled My anger; it will burn forever.” (17:4).
This is what the LORD says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes mere flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD. (17:5).
He will be like a shrub in the desert; he will not see when prosperity comes. He will dwell in the parched places of the desert, in a salt land where no one lives. (17:6).
But blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose confidence is in Him. (17:7).

He is like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream. It does not fear when the heat comes, and its leaves are always green. It does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit. (17:8).
The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it? (17:9).
I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve. (17:10).
Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly. In the middle of his days his riches will desert him, and in the end he will be the fool.” (17:11).
A glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary. (17:12).
O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who abandon You will be put to shame. All who turn away will be written in the dust, for they have abandoned the LORD, the fountain of living water. (17:13).
Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, for You are my praise. (17:14).
Behold, they keep saying to me, “Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!” (17:15).
But I have not run away from being Your shepherd; I have not desired the day of despair. You know that the utterance of my lips was spoken in Your presence. (17:16).
Do not become a terror to me; You are my refuge in the day of disaster. (17:17).

Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame. Let them be terrified, but do not let me be terrified. Bring upon them the day of disaster and shatter them with double destruction. (17:18).
This is what the LORD said to me: “Go and stand at the gate of the people, through which the kings of Judah go in and out; and stand at all the other gates of Jerusalem. (17:19).
Say to them, ‘Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, all people of Judah and Jerusalem who enter through these gates. (17:20).
This is what the LORD says: Take heed for yourselves; do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. (17:21).
You must not carry a load out of your houses or do any work on the Sabbath day, but you must keep the Sabbath day holy, just as I commanded your forefathers. (17:22).
Yet they would not listen or incline their ear, but they stiffened their necks and would not listen or receive My discipline. (17:23).
If, however, you listen carefully to Me, says the LORD, and bring no load through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, and keep the Sabbath day holy, and do no work on it, (17:24).

then kings and princes will enter through the gates of this city. They will sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses with their officials, along with the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever. (17:25).

And people will come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, and from the foothills, the hill country, and the Negev, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and thank offerings to the house of the LORD. (17:26).

But if you do not listen to Me to keep the Sabbath day holy by not carrying a load while entering the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle an unquenchable fire in its gates to consume the citadels of Jerusalem.’” (17:27).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:15-16: Tablets written by the finger of God, the opposite of the iron pen and diamond point of 17:1.
Psalm 1:1-3: The man who delights in the law is a tree planted by streams of water whose leaf does not wither.
Exodus 20:8-11: The Sabbath command, the statute the gate sermon of 17:19-27 prosecutes.
Nehemiah 13:15-22: Nehemiah shuts Jerusalem's gates before the Sabbath to stop the trade, the enforcement Jeremiah called for.
Deuteronomy 30:15-20: Life and death set before the people, with the charge to choose life.

translationNotes.term: Iron pen with a diamond point
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵט בַּרְזֶל (et barzel) - Hebrew: שָׁמִיר (shamir)
translationNotes.note: Two tools from stone-cutting. An iron stylus scratched soft surfaces; a harder tip, shamir, was needed to cut stone or gemstone, and the same word is used in Ezekiel 3:9 and Zechariah 7:12 for the hardest thing there is. Verse 1 says the sin is engraved this way on the tablet of the heart and on the horns of the altar, meaning it is cut in, not written on.

Four projections rising from the corners of the altar. Blood from a sin offering was smeared on them, as in Leviticus 4:7, and a man in danger of his life could seize them for sanctuary, as Adonijah and Joab do in 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. Verse 1 says the guilt is carved into the very place where guilt was supposed to be dealt with.

Verses 5-8 set two plants side by side. One is a scrub bush in the salt flats and the parched wilderness, which sees no rain and cannot tell when good comes. The other is a tree with roots run out to a watercourse; it does not notice the heat and keeps bearing in a drought year. In a country where the difference between the two is a matter of where the roots reach, the picture needs no explanation.

translationNotes.term: A partridge hatching eggs it did not lay
translationNotes.note: Verse 11 draws on a piece of country lore about the partridge sitting on another bird's clutch and losing the brood when they hatch and go. It is applied to a man who gets rich by injustice and finds it gone by mid-life.

translationNotes.term: Bearing a burden through the gates
translationNotes.note: The Sabbath sermon in 17:19-27 targets one specific act: carrying goods in and out of the city gates on the seventh day. Gates were where markets were held and where produce entered, so a load coming through the gate on the Sabbath means business was open. Nehemiah 13:15-22 later shuts the gates from dusk on the sixth day for exactly this reason.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah declares Judah's sin is permanent and warns that those who trust in flesh rather than the LORD will wither like desert shrubs, while those who trust in him will flourish like trees by water. He then receives instruction to stand at Jerusalem's gates and tell the people to keep the Sabbath holy, promising that obedience will bring prosperity and continued rulership, while disobedience will result in fire consuming the city's fortresses.

headings.text: The Sin and Punishment of Judah

stories.title: 🏺 Jeremiah 18
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: (18:1).
“Go down at once to the potter’s house, and there I will give you My message.” (18:2).
So I went down to the potter’s house and saw him working at the wheel. (18:3).
But the vessel that he was shaping from the clay became flawed in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do. (18:4).
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, (18:5).
“O house of Israel, declares the LORD, can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay? Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel. (18:6).
At any time I might announce that a nation or kingdom will be uprooted, torn down, and destroyed. (18:7).
But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring. (18:8).
And if at another time I announce that I will build up and establish a nation or kingdom, (18:9).
and if it does evil in My sight and does not listen to My voice, then I will relent of the good I had intended for it. (18:10).

Now therefore, tell the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem that this is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, I am planning a disaster for you and devising a plan against you. Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.’ (18:11).
But they will reply, ‘It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.’” (18:12).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: “Inquire among the nations: Who has ever heard things like these? Virgin Israel has done a most terrible thing. (18:13).
Does the snow of Lebanon ever leave its rocky slopes? Or do its cool waters flowing from a distance ever run dry? (18:14).
Yet My people have forgotten Me. They burn incense to worthless idols that make them stumble in their ways, leaving the ancient roads to walk on rutted bypaths instead of on the highway. (18:15).
They have made their land a desolation, a perpetual object of scorn; all who pass by will be appalled and shake their heads. (18:16).
I will scatter them before the enemy like the east wind. I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.” (18:17).

Then some said, “Come, let us make plans against Jeremiah, for the law will never be lost to the priest, nor counsel to the wise, nor an oracle to the prophet. Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” (18:18).
Attend to me, O LORD. Hear what my accusers are saying! (18:19).
Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for me. Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them. (18:20).

Therefore, hand their children over to famine; pour out the power of the sword upon them. Let their wives become childless and widowed; let their husbands be slain by disease, their young men struck down by the sword in battle. (18:21).
Let a cry be heard from their houses when You suddenly bring raiders against them, for they have dug a pit to capture me and have hidden snares for my feet. (18:22).

But You, O LORD, know all their deadly plots against me. Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight. Let them be overthrown before You; deal with them in the time of Your anger. (18:23).
crossRefs: Isaiah 45:9: A woe on the clay that quarrels with the one who shapes it.
Isaiah 64:8: We are the clay and You are our potter, and we are all the work of Your hand.
Romans 9:20-21: Paul takes up the potter and the clay, and the potter's right over the same lump.
Jonah 3:6-10: A nation warned of disaster turns from its evil and God relents, the reversal described in 18:7-8.
Psalm 35:7-8: Enemies dig a pit without cause, the prayer Jeremiah prays in 18:20-22.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew is a dual noun meaning the two stones, and that is what the machine was: two stone discs on a vertical wooden axle set in a socket. The potter kicked or spun the heavy lower disc with his feet and threw the clay on the smaller upper one, keeping both hands free. Stone wheel-heads of exactly this kind turn up in Iron Age Judean towns. Verse 3 says Jeremiah went down and watched a man at work at one.

Verse 4 is a description of ordinary throwing. Clay collapses on the wheel when the walls run thin or off centre, and the potter does not throw it out; he balls it up and starts again while it is still wet. A vessel already fired cannot be reworked, which is the difference between this chapter and the smashed jar of chapter 19.

The verb covers being moved, changing course, and relenting from a stated intention. Verses 7-10 state the principle in both directions: a threatened nation that turns is spared, and a promised nation that turns to evil loses the good. The chapter presents an announced judgment as an announcement, not a sealed verdict.

The Lebanon range north of Israel holds snow on its heights into the summer, and the meltwater feeds cold streams that run all year. Verse 14 uses it as the type of the thing that never fails. Judah forgetting God is set against a mountain that always has snow on it.

Verse 18 lays out the plot in the plotters' own words. They will not touch him; they will attack his standing, since law, counsel and the word are supposed to come from the priest, the wise man and the prophet. Discredit the prophet and the office covers the rest.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah visits a potter's house and receives a message that God shapes nations like clay, able to reverse judgment if they repent or withdraw blessing if they turn to evil; Jeremiah warns Judah to reform or face disaster, but the people refuse, and Jeremiah then calls on God to punish those plotting against him.

stories.title: 🏺 Jeremiah 19
summaryBullets: This is what the LORD says: “Go and buy a clay jar from a potter. Take some of the elders of the people and leaders of the priests, (19:1).
and go out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom near the entrance of the Potsherd Gate. Proclaim there the words I speak to you, (19:2).

saying, ‘Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and residents of Jerusalem. This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am going to bring such disaster on this place that the ears of all who hear of it will ring, (19:3).

because they have abandoned Me and made this a foreign place. They have burned incense in this place to other gods that neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have ever known. They have filled this place with the blood of the innocent. (19:4).
They have built high places to Baal on which to burn their children in the fire as offerings to Baal — something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind. (19:5).
So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place will no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. (19:6).

And in this place I will ruin the plans of Judah and Jerusalem. I will make them fall by the sword before their enemies, by the hands of those who seek their lives, and I will give their carcasses as food to the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. (19:7).
I will make this city a desolation and an object of scorn. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds. (19:8).
I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and they will eat one another’s flesh in the siege and distress inflicted on them by their enemies who seek their lives.’ (19:9).
Then you are to shatter the jar in the presence of the men who accompany you, (19:10).

and you are to proclaim to them that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I will shatter this nation and this city, like one shatters a potter’s jar that can never again be repaired. They will bury the dead in Topheth until there is no more room to bury them. (19:11).
This is what I will do to this place and to its residents, declares the LORD. I will make this city like Topheth. (19:12).

The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah will be defiled like that place, Topheth— all the houses on whose rooftops they burned incense to all the host of heaven and poured out drink offerings to other gods.” (19:13).
Then Jeremiah returned from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and proclaimed to all the people, (19:14).

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I am about to bring on this city and on all the villages around it every disaster I have pronounced against them, because they have stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words.’” (19:15).
crossRefs: Leviticus 18:21: The statute forbidding a man to give any of his children to Molech and so profane God's name.
Leviticus 20:2-5: Death by stoning for anyone in Israel who gives his children to Molech, and judgment on those who look away.
2 Kings 21:5-6: Manasseh burns his own son in the fire and fills Jerusalem with innocent blood.
Deuteronomy 28:53-57: Parents eating their own children under siege, the horror 19:9 says is coming.
Psalm 2:9: A ruler breaks the nations like a potter's vessel, the same act Jeremiah performs in 19:10-11.

translationNotes.term: Topheth and the burning of children
translationNotes.note: The burning place in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, immediately outside Jerusalem's southern wall. Verse 5 says plainly what was done there: high places built to Baal on which they burned their children in the fire. Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5 make it a capital offence, 2 Kings 16:3 and 21:6 record two kings of Judah doing it to their own sons, and 2 Kings 23:10 records Josiah destroying the site. The Greek name of this valley is Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for hell.

A gate on the south side of Jerusalem named for broken pottery, opening toward the Hinnom valley where the city's rubbish and its kiln waste went. Jeremiah is told in 19:2 to carry a new jar out through the gate named for smashed ones, and to smash it there.

translationNotes.term: A potter's jar that can never be repaired
translationNotes.note: The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the glug of liquid poured from a narrow neck. Verse 1 has him buy it, not make it, so it is already fired. A fired vessel cannot be reworked on the wheel the way the wet clay of 18:4 could. That is the difference the two chapters are built on, and 19:11 states it: shattered so that it can never again be repaired.

translationNotes.term: Elders and senior priests as witnesses
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 tells Jeremiah to take elders of the people and leading priests out with him. These were the men who ran the city's legal business and its temple. Bringing them to the site meant the act was performed in front of the officials who could not later claim they had not seen it.

translationNotes.term: Rooftop incense to the host of heaven
translationNotes.note: Judean houses had flat roofs used for sleeping, drying, and storage, reached by an outside stair. Verse 13 says every one of those roofs had incense burned on it to the stars. Astral worship put an altar on top of an ordinary family home, which is what makes the count in that verse so large.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah buys a clay jar, takes elders and priests to the Valley of Ben Hinnom, and breaks the jar while pronouncing God's judgment - disaster, siege, cannibalism, and devastation for Judah and Jerusalem because they have forsaken God for foreign gods and burned their children as offerings to Baal. He then returns to the temple court and reiterates the pronouncement to all the people.

stories.title: 🏺 Jeremiah 20
summaryBullets: When Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer and the chief official in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things, (20:1).
he had Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD. (20:2).
The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, “The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib. (20:3).

For this is what the LORD says: ‘I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies before your very eyes. And I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon, and he will carry them away to Babylon and put them to the sword. (20:4).

I will give away all the wealth of this city — all its products and valuables, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah — to their enemies. They will plunder them, seize them, and carry them off to Babylon. (20:5).

And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity. You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried — you and all your friends to whom you have prophesied these lies.’” (20:6).
You have deceived me, O LORD, and I was deceived. You have overcome me and prevailed. I am a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me. (20:7).
For whenever I speak, I cry out; I proclaim violence and destruction. For the word of the LORD has become to me a reproach and derision all day long. (20:8).

If I say, “I will not mention Him or speak any more in His name,” His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail. (20:9).

For I have heard the whispering of many: “Terror is on every side! Report him; let us report him!” All my trusted friends watch for my fall: “Perhaps he will be deceived so that we may prevail against him and take our vengeance upon him.” (20:10).

But the LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior. Therefore, my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail. Since they have not succeeded, they will be utterly put to shame, with an everlasting disgrace that will never be forgotten. (20:11).
O LORD of Hosts, who examines the righteous, who sees the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause. (20:12).
Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD! For He rescues the life of the needy from the hands of evildoers. (20:13).
Cursed be the day I was born! May the day my mother bore me never be blessed. (20:14).
Cursed be the man who brought my father the news, saying, “A son is born to you,” bringing him great joy. (20:15).
May that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without compassion. May he hear an outcry in the morning and a battle cry at noon, (20:16).
because he did not kill me in the womb so that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb forever enlarged. (20:17).
Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame? (20:18).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 29:24-28: The temple overseer's authority to put a raving prophet in stocks and neck irons, the office Pashhur held.
Jeremiah 1:18-19: The promise that they would fight him and not prevail, tested here for the first time.
Psalm 31:13: Terror on every side appears as a set phrase, the name Jeremiah gives Pashhur in 20:3.
Job 3:1-11: Job curses the day of his birth in the same terms Jeremiah uses in 20:14-18.
Acts 5:40-42: Apostles are flogged and ordered to stop speaking, and do not stop, the compulsion of 20:9 in another setting.

translationNotes.term: Chief officer in the house of the LORD
translationNotes.note: Pashhur held the temple police post, the officer responsible for order in the courts. 29:26 describes the duty exactly: to put any madman who acts the prophet into stocks and neck irons. He is not acting outside his authority in 20:2, which is the point. The system worked as designed and it was aimed at the true prophet.

The name comes from the verb to twist or overturn. It was a frame that clamped the neck, wrists and ankles together and forced the body into a bent position, so the punishment was cramp and exposure as well as restraint. It was set up at the Benjamin Gate, a public thoroughfare, so the shame was the greater part of the sentence.

Terror on Every Side. Jeremiah renames Pashhur in 20:3, and renaming a man was a claim on his future, the way Abram becomes Abraham. The same phrase turns up as a stock cry of panic in 6:25, 46:5, 49:29 and Psalm 31:13, so the new name is the sound of a city under attack, fastened to the man who ran the temple police.

translationNotes.term: Fire shut up in my bones
translationNotes.note: Verses 7-9 are the sharpest of the passages where Jeremiah argues with God. He says he was persuaded and overpowered, that he resolved to stop speaking, and that holding it in became unbearable. The compulsion is presented as physical, not devotional.

translationNotes.term: Cursed be the day I was born
translationNotes.note: Verses 14-18 end the chapter without resolution, and the book leaves them there. The wording tracks Job 3:3-11 closely, down to cursing the man who brought the news of the birth. Both passages are complaints preserved in Scripture as spoken, with no correction attached.

stories.keyTakeaway: Pashhur beats Jeremiah and stocks him; when released, Jeremiah pronounces that Pashhur will be called Terror on Every Side and will go into exile to Babylon. Jeremiah then laments that God's word compels him to speak despite ridicule and danger, though he trusts the LORD will vindicate him and ultimately curses the day he was born.

stories.title: 🧭 Jeremiah 21
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchijah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah. They said, (21:1).

“Please inquire of the LORD on our behalf, since Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is waging war against us. Perhaps the LORD will perform for us something like all His past wonders, so that Nebuchadnezzar will withdraw from us.” (21:2).
But Jeremiah answered, “You are to tell Zedekiah that (21:3).

this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I will turn against you the weapons of war in your hands, with which you are fighting the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who besiege you outside the wall, and I will assemble their forces in the center of this city. (21:4).
And I Myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm, with anger, fury, and great wrath. (21:5).
I will strike down the residents of this city, both man and beast. They will die in a terrible plague.’ (21:6).

‘After that,’ declares the LORD, ‘I will hand over Zedekiah king of Judah, his officers, and the people in this city who survive the plague and sword and famine, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to their enemies who seek their lives. He will put them to the sword; he will not spare them or show pity or compassion.’ (21:7).
Furthermore, you are to tell this people that this is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. (21:8).

Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague, but whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who besiege you will live; he will retain his life like a spoil of war. (21:9).
For I have set My face against this city to bring disaster and not good, declares the LORD. It will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will destroy it with fire.’ (21:10).
Moreover, tell the house of the king of Judah to hear the word of the LORD. (21:11).

O house of David, this is what the LORD says: ‘Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor, or My wrath will go forth like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it because of their evil deeds. (21:12).
Behold, I am against you who dwell above the valley, atop the rocky plateau — declares the LORD — you who say, “Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?” (21:13).
I will punish you as your deeds deserve, declares the LORD. I will kindle a fire in your forest that will consume everything around you.’” (21:14).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:1-3: Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem, the siege Zedekiah is sending to ask about.
Jeremiah 37:3-10: The same king sends the same priest Zephaniah a second time and gets the same answer.
Deuteronomy 30:15-19: Life and death, blessing and curse, set before the people to choose.
Exodus 23:6-9: The law commanding justice for the poor and the sojourner, the charge behind 21:12.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The promise to David's house, which 21:11-14 warns will not shield an unjust king.

translationNotes.term: Inquire of the LORD for us
translationNotes.note: A formal request for an oracle before a battle, standard royal procedure; David does it repeatedly in 1 Samuel 23 and 30. Zedekiah is following the correct process in 21:2, and expecting the answer his ancestors got at 2 Kings 19:32-34 when Assyria besieged the same city and withdrew. The answer he gets is the reverse.

translationNotes.term: The way of life and the way of death
translationNotes.note: Verses 8-9 are not a general proverb. In this one situation, under this one siege, staying in the city is the way of death and going out to surrender is the way of life. It amounts to telling citizens to desert, which is exactly the charge the officials bring against Jeremiah in 38:4.

A soldier's idiom. Plunder is what you carry off a battlefield, so getting your life as plunder means coming out with nothing except being alive. It recurs at 38:2, 39:18 and 45:5, always to a person who survives a disaster with everything else gone.

The second priest under the high priest, named in 52:24 among the officials executed at Riblah after the city fell. He appears as the king's envoy here and again in 37:3, and in 29:25-29 he receives the Babylonian letter demanding Jeremiah be silenced and reads it to Jeremiah instead.

Verse 12 is addressed to the royal house. Legal cases were heard at first light in the gate or the palace court, before the day's heat, so justice in the morning is the king's daily working duty, not a figure of speech. 2 Samuel 15:2 shows Absalom exploiting the same morning session.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Zedekiah sends officials to ask Jeremiah if God will deliver Jerusalem from the Babylonian siege, but Jeremiah announces that God will instead turn the city's weapons against it, strike down its people with plague, and hand survivors over to Nebuchadnezzar. He offers the people a choice between staying in the city to die or surrendering to the Babylonians to live, and warns the royal house that God will punish Jerusalem with fire for its injustice.

headings.text: A Message to the House of David

stories.title: 🧭 Jeremiah 22
summaryBullets: This is what the LORD says: “Go down to the palace of the king of Judah and proclaim this message there, (22:1).
saying, ‘Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David— you and your officials and your people who enter these gates. (22:2).

This is what the LORD says: Administer justice and righteousness. Rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor. Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow. Do not shed innocent blood in this place. (22:3).

For if you will indeed carry out these commands, then kings who sit on David’s throne will enter through the gates of this palace riding on chariots and horses — they and their officials and their people. (22:4).
But if you do not obey these words, then I swear by Myself, declares the LORD, that this house will become a pile of rubble.’” (22:5).

For this is what the LORD says concerning the house of the king of Judah: “You are like Gilead to Me, like the summit of Lebanon; but I will surely turn you into a desert, like cities that are uninhabited. (22:6).
I will appoint destroyers against you, each man with his weapons, and they will cut down the choicest of your cedars and throw them into the fire. (22:7).
And many nations will pass by this city and ask one another, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this great city?’ (22:8).
Then people will reply, ‘Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and have worshiped and served other gods.’” (22:9).
Do not weep for him who is dead; do not mourn his loss. Weep bitterly for him who is exiled, for he will never return to see his native land. (22:10).
For this is what the LORD says concerning Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who succeeded his father Josiah but has gone forth from this place: “He will never return, (22:11).
but he will die in the place to which he was exiled; he will never see this land again.” (22:12).
“Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms without justice, who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages, (22:13).
who says, ‘I will build myself a great palace, with spacious upper rooms.’ So he cuts windows in it, panels it with cedar, and paints it with vermilion. (22:14).
Does it make you a king to excel in cedar? Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness, and so it went well with him. (22:15).
He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?” declares the LORD. (22:16).
“But your eyes and heart are set on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.” (22:17).

Therefore this is what the LORD says concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah: “They will not mourn for him: ‘Alas, my brother! Alas, my sister!’ They will not mourn for him: ‘Alas, my master! Alas, his splendor!’ (22:18).
He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem. (22:19).
Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers have been crushed. (22:20).
I warned you when you were secure. You said, ‘I will not listen.’ This has been your way from youth, that you have not obeyed My voice. (22:21).
The wind will drive away all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity. Then you will be ashamed and humiliated because of all your wickedness. (22:22).
O inhabitant of Lebanon, nestled in the cedars, how you will groan when pangs of anguish come upon you, agony like a woman in labor.” (22:23).
“As surely as I live,” declares the LORD, “evenif you, Coniah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, were a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off. (22:24).
In fact, I will hand you over to those you dread, who want to take your life — to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans. (22:25).
I will hurl you and the mother who gave you birth into another land, where neither of you were born — and there you both will die. (22:26).
You will never return to the land for which you long.” (22:27).
Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants? Why are he and his descendants hurled out and cast into a land they do not know? (22:28).
O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD! (22:29).

This is what the LORD says: “Enroll this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime. None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.” (22:30).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 24:14-15: A hired worker must be paid before sundown on the day he works, the statute Jehoiakim breaks in 22:13.
2 Kings 23:31-34: Jehoahaz reigns three months, is deposed by Pharaoh Neco and dies in Egypt; the Shallum of 22:11-12.
2 Kings 24:1-6: Jehoiakim's reign, rebellion and death, the king condemned in 22:13-19.
2 Kings 24:8-16: Jehoiachin surrenders and is carried to Babylon with his mother, the Coniah of 22:24-30.
Matthew 1:11-12: Jeconiah stands in the line from David to Joseph, between Josiah and Shealtiel.

translationNotes.note: Judah's last kings each carry more than one name, which makes the chapter hard to follow. Shallum in 22:11 is Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, deposed after three months. Coniah in 22:24 is Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah in Matthew 1:11. Throne names were assigned at accession, sometimes by the foreign king doing the appointing, as 2 Kings 23:34 and 24:17 both record.

Cedar came by sea from Lebanon and was the most expensive building timber in the region, used for Solomon's temple and palace. Vermilion is a red pigment from mercury ore, used to paint panelling. Verse 14 lists them as the marks of a palace built with unpaid labour, which is why the next verse asks whether cedar makes a king.

Verse 19 says Jehoiakim will be dragged out and thrown beyond the gates of Jerusalem. A dead pack animal was hauled outside the walls and left. For a king of Judah, who expected a tomb among his fathers in the city of David, this is the announcement that there will be no tomb and no mourning.

A carved seal, worn on the hand or on a cord, pressed into wet clay to seal documents and jars. It was the owner's legal signature and never left him. Verse 24 says that even if Coniah were the signet on God's right hand, He would pull it off. Haggai 2:23 later says the opposite of Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin's grandson.

translationNotes.term: Write this man down as childless
translationNotes.note: Verse 30 explains its own terms in the same breath: none of his offspring will prosper, sitting on David's throne and ruling in Judah. Jehoiachin had sons, listed in 1 Chronicles 3:17-18, and 52:31-34 has him alive and eating at the Babylonian king's table. The sentence is about the throne, not about descendants.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah delivers judgment against the Judean royal palace and successive kings, warning that disobedience will bring ruin, exile, and disgrace, with specific condemnation of Jehoiakim's oppression and Jehoiachin's removal from power. The palace will become a wasteland, the kings will lose their thrones, and none of Jehoiachin's descendants will rule Judah again.

stories.title: 🧭 Jeremiah 23
summaryBullets: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” declares the LORD. (23:1).

Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the shepherds who tend My people: “You have scattered My flock and driven them away, and have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds, declares the LORD. (23:2).
Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them, and I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply. (23:3).
I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing, declares the LORD. (23:4).
Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land. (23:5).
In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness. (23:6).
So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they will no longer say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.’ (23:7).

Instead they will say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.’ Then they will dwell once more in their own land.” (23:8).
As for the prophets: My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble. I have become like a drunkard, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD, because of His holy words. (23:9).
For the land is full of adulterers — because of the curse, the land mourns and the pastures of the wilderness have dried up — their course is evil and their power is misused. (23:10).
“For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness,” declares the LORD. (23:11).
“Therefore their path will become slick; they will be driven away into the darkness and fall into it. For I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD. (23:12).
“Among the prophets of Samaria I saw an offensive thing: They prophesied by Baal and led My people Israel astray. (23:13).

And among the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: They commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns his back on wickedness. They are all like Sodom to Me; the people of Jerusalem are like Gomorrah.” (23:14).

Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says concerning the prophets: “I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has spread throughout the land.” (23:15).

This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. (23:16).
They keep saying to those who despise Me, ‘The LORD says that you will have peace,’ and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart, ‘No harm will come to you.’ (23:17).
But which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word? Who has given heed to His word and obeyed it? (23:18).
Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked. (23:19).
The anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart. In the days to come you will understand this clearly. (23:20).
I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message; I did not speak to them, yet they have prophesied. (23:21).
But if they had stood in My council, they would have proclaimed My words to My people and turned them back from their evil ways and deeds.” (23:22).
“Am I only a God nearby,” declares the LORD, “and not a God far away?” (23:23).
“Can a man hide in secret places where I cannot see him?” declares the LORD. “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” declares the LORD. (23:24).
“I have heard the sayings of the prophets who prophesy lies in My name: ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’ (23:25).
How long will this continue in the hearts of these prophets who prophesy falsehood, these prophets of the delusion of their own minds? (23:26).
They suppose the dreams that they tell one another will make My people forget My name, just as their fathers forgot My name through the worship of Baal. (23:27).
Let the prophet who has a dream retell it, but let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” declares the LORD. (23:28).
“Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?” (23:29).
“Therefore behold,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who steal from one another words they attribute to Me.” (23:30).
“Yes,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who wag their own tongues and proclaim, ‘The LORD declares it.’” (23:31).

“Indeed,” declares the LORD, “I am against those who prophesy false dreams and retell them to lead My people astray with their reckless lies. It was not I who sent them or commanded them, and they are of no benefit at all to these people,” declares the LORD. (23:32).
“Now when this people or a prophet or priest asks you, ‘What is the burden of the LORD?’ you are to say to them, ‘What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD.’ (23:33).
As for the prophet or priest or anyone who claims, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ I will punish that man and his household. (23:34).
This is what each man is to say to his friend and to his brother: ‘What has the LORD answered?’ or ‘What has the LORD spoken?’ (23:35).
But refer no more to the burden of the LORD, for each man’s word becomes the burden, so that you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of Hosts, our God. (23:36).
Thus you are to say to the prophet: ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and ‘What has the LORD spoken?’ (23:37).

But if you claim, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ then this is what the LORD says: Because you have said, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ and I specifically told you not to make this claim, (23:38).
therefore I will surely forget you and will cast you out of My presence, both you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. (23:39).
And I will bring upon you everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation that will never be forgotten.” (23:40).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 34:1-16: Woe to shepherds who feed themselves, and God's pledge to search out the flock Himself.
Isaiah 11:1-5: A shoot from the stump of Jesse who judges the poor with righteousness.
Jeremiah 33:15-16: The Righteous Branch promised again, with the name carried over to the city.
Deuteronomy 18:20: A prophet who presumes to speak in God's name what He did not command must die.
John 10:11-16: Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life and brings other sheep into one flock.

translationNotes.note: Standard ancient Near Eastern language for rulers, used of kings in Babylonian and Assyrian royal inscriptions as well as in Israel. The shepherds of 23:1-2 are Judah's kings and officials, the men chapter 22 has just named. The job description is in the complaint: they scattered the flock, drove it away, and did not attend to it.

Branch means a fresh shoot from a cut stump, the growth that comes back after a tree has been felled. Verse 5 uses it of a king raised up for David after the dynasty has been cut down. The same title appears in Isaiah 11:1, Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12.

The name given the coming king in 23:6. It is a pointed choice: the reigning king as Jeremiah speaks is Zedekiah, whose name means the LORD is my righteousness. In 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem itself.

translationNotes.term: Standing in the council of the LORD
translationNotes.note: The word means a confidential circle and the private talk that goes on in it. Verses 18 and 22 make it the test of a true prophet: has he stood in that circle and heard, or is he repeating what he dreamed and what he heard from the next prophet along, as 23:30 charges.

One Hebrew word means both an oracle and a load carried on the back. Verses 33-40 turn on the pun. People were asking what the LORD's burden is, using the word as a catchphrase; the answer in 23:33 is that they are the burden, and the phrase is then banned outright because it had become a way of dressing up any message as divine.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD condemns the shepherds and false prophets of Judah for scattering his flock and speaking lies in his name, promising judgment on them while assuring that he will gather his remnant and raise up a righteous Branch from David. He warns the people not to listen to these false prophets who speak visions from their own minds rather than from his mouth.

stories.title: 🌿 Jeremiah 24
summaryBullets: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, as well as the officials of Judah and the craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD. (24:1).
One basket had very good figs, like those that ripen early, but the other basket contained very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten. (24:2).
“Jeremiah,” the LORD asked, “what do you see?” “Figs!” I replied. “The good figs are very good, but the bad figs are very bad, so bad they cannot be eaten.” (24:3).
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, (24:4).
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans. (24:5).
I will keep My eyes on them for good and will return them to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them. (24:6).
I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the LORD. They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart. (24:7).

But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten,’ says the LORD, ‘so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem— those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt. (24:8).
I will make them a horror and an offense to all the kingdoms of the earth, a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them. (24:9).
And I will send against them sword and famine and plague, until they have perished from the land that I gave to them and their fathers.’” (24:10).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 24:10-16: Jehoiachin, the officials, the craftsmen and the smiths carried to Babylon, the good figs of 24:1.
Jeremiah 29:4-7: The letter telling those same exiles to build houses and seek the welfare of the city.
Ezekiel 11:14-20: God tells those left in Jerusalem that He has been a sanctuary to the exiles, and promises them one heart.
Deuteronomy 30:6: God will circumcise their heart so they love Him, matching the heart to know Him in 24:7.
Jeremiah 44:11-14: The Judeans who fled to Egypt, the third group 24:8 consigns to the sword.

translationNotes.term: Two baskets set before the temple
translationNotes.note: Baskets of first-ripe produce were carried to the sanctuary and set down in front of it as an offering, the rite laid out in Deuteronomy 26:1-4. The vision borrows that scene and puts two baskets there, one fit to present and one that has gone bad, so the judgment is passed in the language of an inspection at the temple door.

The fig tree in Judah gives an early crop in June from the previous year's wood and the main crop in late summer. The early figs were the prized ones, eaten fresh and gone quickly. Verse 2 calls one basket by that name, which makes the other basket not merely inferior but inedible.

Verse 1 fixes the date: after Nebuchadnezzar carried off Jeconiah, the officials, the craftsmen and the metalworkers. 2 Kings 24:14-16 gives the numbers and says the poorest people of the land were left. The vision reverses the obvious reading of that event. The ones taken away are the good basket, and the ones left in Jerusalem are not.

Verse 7 states the promise in its plainest form: I will give them a heart to know Me, and they will be My people and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with their whole heart. The same pledge is expanded in 31:33-34 and 32:38-40, and Deuteronomy 30:6 gives it first.

stories.keyTakeaway: God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs - one good, one spoiled - and explains that the exiles taken to Babylon will be preserved and restored, while Zedekiah and those remaining in Jerusalem or Egypt will face destruction.

stories.title: 🌿 Jeremiah 25
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, which was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. (25:1).
So the prophet Jeremiah spoke to all the people of Judah and all the residents of Jerusalem as follows: (25:2).

“From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah until this very day— twenty-three years— the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken to you again and again, but you have not listened. (25:3).
And the LORD has sent all His servants the prophets to you again and again, but you have not listened or inclined your ear to hear. (25:4).
The prophets told you, ‘Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways and deeds, and you can dwell in the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers forever and ever. (25:5).
Do not follow other gods to serve and worship them, and do not provoke Me to anger with the works of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.’ (25:6).
‘But to your own harm, you have not listened to Me,’ declares the LORD, ‘so you have provoked Me to anger with the works of your hands.’ (25:7).
Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Because you have not obeyed My words, (25:8).

behold, I will summon all the families of the north, declares the LORD, and I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, whom I will bring against this land, against its residents, and against all the surrounding nations. So I will devote them to destruction and make them an object of horror and contempt, an everlasting desolation. (25:9).
Moreover, I will banish from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp. (25:10).
And this whole land will become a desolate wasteland, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. (25:11).

But when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt, declares the LORD, and I will make it an everlasting desolation. (25:12).
I will bring upon that land all the words I have pronounced against it, all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah has prophesied against all the nations. (25:13).
For many nations and great kings will enslave them, and I will repay them according to their deeds and according to the work of their hands.’” (25:14).
This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it. (25:15).
And they will drink and stagger and go out of their minds, because of the sword that I will send among them.” (25:16).
So I took the cup from the LORD’s hand and made all the nations drink from it, each one to whom the LORD had sent me, (25:17).
to make them a ruin, an object of horror and contempt and cursing, as they are to this day — Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials; (25:18).
Pharaoh king of Egypt, his officials, his leaders, and all his people; (25:19).
all the mixed tribes; all the kings of Uz; all the kings of the Philistines: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod; (25:20).
Edom, Moab, and the Ammonites; (25:21).
all the kings of Tyre and Sidon; the kings of the coastlands across the sea; (25:22).
Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair; (25:23).
all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert; (25:24).
all the kings of Zimri, Elam, and Media; (25:25).
all the kings of the north, both near and far, one after another — all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. And after all of them, the king of Sheshach will drink it too. (25:26).

“Then you are to tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Drink, get drunk, and vomit. Fall down and never get up again, because of the sword I will send among you.’ (25:27).
If they refuse to take the cup from your hand and drink it, you are to tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘You most certainly must drink it! (25:28).

For behold, I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name, so how could you possibly go unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of Hosts.’ (25:29).

So you are to prophesy all these words against them and say to them: ‘The LORD will roar from on high; He will raise His voice from His holy habitation. He will roar loudly over His pasture; like those who tread the grapes, He will call out with a shout against all the inhabitants of the earth. (25:30).

The tumult will resound to the ends of the earth because the LORD brings a charge against the nations. He brings judgment on all mankind and puts the wicked to the sword,’” declares the LORD. (25:31).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Behold! Disaster is spreading from nation to nation; a mighty storm is rising from the ends of the earth.” (25:32).
Those slain by the LORD on that day will be spread from one end of the earth to the other. They will not be mourned, gathered, or buried. They will be like dung lying on the ground. (25:33).
Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock. For the days of your slaughter have come; you will fall and be shattered like fine pottery. (25:34).
Flight will evade the shepherds, and escape will elude the leaders of the flock. (25:35).
Hear the cry of the shepherds, the wailing of the leaders of the flock, for the LORD is destroying their pasture. (25:36).
The peaceful meadows have been silenced because of the LORD’s burning anger. (25:37).
He has left His den like a lion, for their land has been made a desolation by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD. (25:38).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 24:1-2: Nebuchadnezzar comes up and Jehoiakim serves him three years, the year 25:1 dates this oracle to.
2 Chronicles 36:20-21: The land keeps its sabbaths for seventy years until the kingdom of Persia comes to power.
Daniel 9:2: Daniel reads in Jeremiah the number of years for Jerusalem's desolation, and prays.
Ezra 1:1-4: In Cyrus's first year the LORD stirs him to send the exiles home, at the end of the seventy years.
Psalm 75:8: A cup in the LORD's hand with foaming wine, drained to the dregs by the wicked of the earth.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 gives a double date, the fourth year of Jehoiakim and the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, which lands on 605 BC. That is the year Babylon destroyed the Egyptian army at Carchemish, named in 46:2, and the year the first Judeans were taken to Babylon according to Daniel 1:1. Double-dating an oracle by two kings is how a scribe pinned it to a year everyone could check.

Verse 3 counts from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the year of writing. From about 627 BC to 605 BC is twenty-three years, and the book's own opening date in 1:2 matches. The number is a working total of how long Jeremiah had been preaching without a hearing.

Verses 11-12 give a fixed term for Babylonian dominance, not a round gesture. Counted from the first deportation in 605 BC to Cyrus's decree in 538 BC it runs sixty-seven or sixty-eight years; counted from the temple's destruction in 586 BC to its rebuilding in 516 BC it runs seventy. 2 Chronicles 36:21 ties the number to the land's unkept sabbath years, and Daniel 9:2 treats it as a countable figure and reads it as one.

Verses 15-29 use a courtroom and banquet image at once. The cup is passed round a table of named nations, from Egypt at one end to Babylon at the last, and every one of them must drink. Forced drinking meant staggering, vomiting and falling, which 25:27 spells out. Isaiah 51:17, Psalm 75:8 and Revelation 14:10 use the same cup.

A code name for Babylon in 25:26 and 51:41, produced by the letter-swap called Atbash, where the first letter of the alphabet stands for the last, the second for the second-last, and so on. Applied to Babel it yields Sheshach. The cipher lets the oracle name Babylon last while the list is being read in Babylonian territory.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah recounts twenty-three years of unheeded warnings to Judah and announces that God will send Nebuchadnezzar to destroy the land and its nations; he then symbolically distributes a cup of God's wrath to all the surrounding peoples, from Egypt to Babylon, declaring judgment will spread across the earth.

stories.title: 🏛️ Jeremiah 26
summaryBullets: At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came from the LORD: (26:1).

“This is what the LORD says: Stand in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and speak all the words I have commanded you to speak to all the cities of Judah who come to worship there. Do not omit a word. (26:2).
Perhaps they will listen and turn— each from his evil way of life— so that I may relent of the disaster I am planning to bring upon them because of the evil of their deeds. (26:3).
And you are to tell them that this is what the LORD says: ‘If you do not listen to Me and walk in My law, which I have set before you, (26:4).
and if you do not listen to the words of My servants the prophets, whom I have sent you again and again even though you did not listen, (26:5).
then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth.’” (26:6).
Now the priests and prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD, (26:7).
and as soon as he had finished telling all the people everything the LORD had commanded him to say, the priests and prophets and all the people seized him, shouting, “You must surely die! (26:8).
