How dare you prophesy in the name of the LORD that this house will become like Shiloh and this city will be desolate and deserted!” And all the people assembled against Jeremiah in the house of the LORD. (26:9).
When the officials of Judah heard these things, they went up from the king’s palace to the house of the LORD and sat there at the entrance of the New Gate. (26:10).
Then the priests and prophets said to the officials and all the people, “This man is worthy of death, for he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears!” (26:11).
But Jeremiah said to all the officials and all the people, “The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard. (26:12).
So now, correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, so that He might relent of the disaster He has pronounced against you. (26:13).
As for me, here I am in your hands; do to me what you think is good and right. (26:14).

But know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents; for truly the LORD has sent me to speak all these words in your hearing.” (26:15).
Then the officials and all the people told the priests and prophets, “This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!” (26:16).
Some of the elders of the land stood up and said to the whole assembly of the people, (26:17).

“Micah the Moreshite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and told all the people of Judah that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge.’ (26:18).

Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death? Did Hezekiah not fear the LORD and seek His favor, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster He had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great harm on ourselves!” (26:19).

Now there was another man prophesying in the name of the LORD, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land the same things that Jeremiah did. (26:20).
King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and officials heard his words, and the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah found out about it, he fled in fear and went to Egypt. (26:21).
Then King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt: Elnathan son of Achbor along with some other men. (26:22).
They brought Uriah out of Egypt and took him to King Jehoiakim, who had him put to the sword and his body thrown into the burial place of the common people. (26:23).
Nevertheless, Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death. (26:24).
crossRefs: Micah 3:12: Zion plowed as a field and the temple hill a wooded height, the verse the elders quote in court.
2 Kings 18:1-6: Hezekiah's reforms, the king whose response to Micah the elders cite as precedent.
2 Kings 22:12-14: Ahikam son of Shaphan sent to the prophetess Huldah with the found law book; he shields Jeremiah in 26:24.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22: The law under which the priests demand Jeremiah's death for speaking falsely in the LORD's name.
Matthew 23:34-37: Jesus speaks of prophets sent to Jerusalem and killed there, the pattern Uriah's death shows in 26:20-23.

translationNotes.term: A trial in the temple gate
translationNotes.note: Verses 10-16 are a court sitting, not a riot. The officials come up from the palace and take their seats in the entrance of the New Gate, which is where legal business was heard. The priests and prophets act as prosecutors, Jeremiah answers for himself, and the officials and the people give the verdict. Gates were the courthouses of an Israelite town.

The sanctuary town about twenty miles (32 km) north of Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood through the era of the judges and where Samuel was raised, before Jerusalem existed as a worship centre. It fell after the ark was captured in 1 Samuel 4, and Psalm 78:60 says God forsook the dwelling at Shiloh. Verse 6 is the sentence that gets Jeremiah arrested, because it says the same can happen to this house.

The prophet whose book stands in the Twelve. Verses 18-19 quote Micah 3:12 word for word and date it to Hezekiah's reign, about a century earlier, then note that Hezekiah did not kill him but feared the LORD. This is the earliest recorded instance of one Old Testament prophet's writing being cited in court as a precedent.

Verses 20-23 record a prophet who said the same thing Jeremiah said, fled to Egypt, was extradited by Jehoiakim's men, killed with the sword and thrown into a commoners' burial pit. The account is placed immediately after Jeremiah's acquittal to show the acquittal was not the rule.

Shaphan was Josiah's secretary of state, the man who read the recovered law book to the king in 2 Kings 22:8-10. His sons and grandsons run through Jeremiah as the prophet's protectors: Ahikam saves his life here, Gedaliah son of Ahikam becomes governor in chapter 40, Gemariah lends his chamber for the scroll reading in 36:10, and Elasah carries the letter to Babylon in 29:3.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah delivers God's warning in the temple courtyard, telling Judah to repent or face destruction like Shiloh; priests and prophets seize him demanding death, but officials and people defend him after he speaks directly to them, and Ahikam protects him from execution.

headings.text: A Warning to the Cities of Judah

stories.title: 🏛️ Jeremiah 27
summaryBullets: At the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD. (27:1).
This is what the LORD said to me: “Make for yourself a yoke out of leather straps and put it on your neck. (27:2).
Send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon through the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah. (27:3).
Give them a message from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, to relay to their masters: (27:4).
By My great power and outstretched arm, I made the earth and the men and beasts on the face of it, and I give it to whom I please. (27:5).
So now I have placed all these lands under the authority of My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. I have even made the beasts of the field subject to him. (27:6).
All nations will serve him and his son and grandson, until the time of his own land comes; then many nations and great kings will enslave him. (27:7).

As for the nation or kingdom that does not serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and does not place its neck under his yoke, I will punish that nation by sword and famine and plague, declares the LORD, until I have destroyed it by his hand. (27:8).
But as for you, do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your interpreters of dreams, your mediums, or your sorcerers who declare, ‘You will not serve the king of Babylon.’ (27:9).
For they prophesy to you a lie that will serve to remove you from your land; I will banish you and you will perish. (27:10).
But the nation that will put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave in its own land, to cultivate it and reside in it, declares the LORD.” (27:11).
And to Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke the same message: “Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon; serve him and his people, and live! (27:12).
Why should you and your people die by sword and famine and plague, as the LORD has decreed against any nation that does not serve the king of Babylon? (27:13).
Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say, ‘You must not serve the king of Babylon,’ for they are prophesying to you a lie. (27:14).
For I have not sent them, declares the LORD, and yet they are prophesying falsely in My name; therefore I will banish you, and you will perish— you and the prophets who prophesy to you.” (27:15).

Then I said to the priests and to all this people, “This is what the LORD says: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Look, very soon now the articles from the house of the LORD will be brought back from Babylon.’ They are prophesying to you a lie. (27:16).
Do not listen to them. Serve the king of Babylon and live! Why should this city become a ruin? (27:17).

If they are indeed prophets and the word of the LORD is with them, let them now plead with the LORD of Hosts that the articles remaining in the house of the LORD, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem, not be taken to Babylon. (27:18).
For this is what the LORD of Hosts says about the pillars, the sea, the bases, and the rest of the articles that remain in this city, (27:19).

which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take when he carried Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem. (27:20).
Yes, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says about the articles that remain in the house of the LORD, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: (27:21).
‘They will be carried to Babylon and will remain there until the day I attend to them again,’ declares the LORD. ‘Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place.’” (27:22).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 28:10-14: Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke off Jeremiah's neck and is told God will make an iron one.
Deuteronomy 28:48: Serving an enemy under an iron yoke on the neck, listed in the covenant curses.
2 Kings 24:13: Nebuchadnezzar strips the temple and cuts up the gold vessels Solomon had made.
Daniel 1:1-2: Vessels from the house of God carried to Shinar and put in the treasury of Nebuchadnezzar's god.
Ezra 1:7-11: Cyrus brings out the temple vessels and has them counted back to Judah, as 27:22 said would happen.

translationNotes.note: Two parts, and 27:2 names both. The bars are the shaped wooden crosspieces that lie over the necks of a pair of oxen; the bonds are the leather straps that lash the bars down under the throat so the animal cannot lift its head out. Jeremiah is told to build a working plough yoke and wear it in public. Hananiah breaks the wooden bars in 28:10, and the answer in 28:13 is iron bars, which cannot be snapped.

Verse 3 lists ambassadors from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon meeting in Jerusalem. That is a war council. Small states around Judah were assembling a coalition to throw off Babylon, and Jeremiah walks into the conference wearing an ox yoke and sends each envoy home with a matching one.

The title in 27:6 is the one used of Moses, David and the prophets. Applied to a foreign king who sacked the temple, it is the most offensive line in the chapter to its first hearers, and it is repeated at 25:9 and 43:10. The text presents Babylon as an instrument under orders with a term set on it, and 27:7 fixes the term at three generations.

translationNotes.term: The vessels of the house of the LORD
translationNotes.note: The bronze and gold implements of temple service: basins, snuffers, sprinkling bowls, lampstands, the pillars. The first deportation in 597 BC took part of them, 2 Kings 24:13. The prophets promised the rest would come straight back; 27:19-22 says the remainder goes too. Ezra 1:9-11 records the return, itemised down to knives and bowls.

The Hebrew of 27:1 reads Jehoiakim, while the body of the chapter addresses Zedekiah in 27:3 and 27:12, and 28:1 places these events in Zedekiah's fourth year, about 594 BC. Some ancient manuscripts read Zedekiah at 27:1 to match. The oracle itself is set squarely in Zedekiah's reign.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah puts a yoke on his neck and sends word to surrounding kings that God will give all their lands to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon; he warns Zedekiah and the people against listening to prophets who promise they will not have to serve the Babylonian king, insisting that submission to Babylon is the only way to survive.

stories.title: 📨 Jeremiah 28
summaryBullets: In the fifth month of that same year, the fourth year, near the beginning of the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah, the prophet Hananiah son of Azzur, who was from Gibeon, said to me in the house of the LORD in the presence of the priests and all the people: (28:1).
“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. (28:2).
Within two years I will restore to this place all the articles of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon removed from here and carried to Babylon. (28:3).

And I will restore to this place Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon,’ declares the LORD, ‘for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.’” (28:4).
Then the prophet Jeremiah replied to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD. (28:5).

“Amen!” Jeremiah said. “May the LORD do so! May the LORD fulfill the words you have prophesied, and may He restore the articles of His house and all the exiles back to this place from Babylon. (28:6).
Nevertheless, listen now to this message I am speaking in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people. (28:7).
The prophets of old who preceded you and me prophesied war, disaster, and plague against many lands and great kingdoms. (28:8).
As for the prophet who prophesies peace, only if the word of the prophet comes true will the prophet be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent.” (28:9).
Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it. (28:10).

And in the presence of all the people Hananiah proclaimed, “This is what the LORD says: ‘In this way, within two years I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon off the neck of all the nations.’” At this, Jeremiah the prophet went on his way. (28:11).
But shortly after Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke off his neck, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (28:12).
“Go and tell Hananiah that this is what the LORD says: ‘You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron.’ (28:13).

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations to make them serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they will serve him. I have even given him control of the beasts of the field.’” (28:14).
Then the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah, “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie. (28:15).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘I am about to remove you from the face of the earth. You will die this year because you have preached rebellion against the LORD.’” (28:16).
And in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died. (28:17).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 18:21-22: How to recognise a word the LORD has not spoken, the test Jeremiah applies in 28:9.
Jeremiah 27:2-11: The wooden yoke Jeremiah wore and the message Hananiah is contradicting.
1 Kings 22:11-28: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes iron horns and promises victory; Micaiah is jailed and proved right.
2 Kings 24:12-16: The exile of Jehoiachin and the temple vessels Hananiah promises will be back within two years.
Numbers 16:28-33: Moses stakes his commission on a sign that has to happen within a set time.

translationNotes.note: Called a prophet throughout the chapter, with no qualifier attached until the verdict in 28:15. He uses the correct formula, thus says the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, and he performs a sign act, exactly as Jeremiah does. Nothing in his method separates him from Jeremiah, which is the difficulty the chapter is built on.

Verse 3 names a deadline. That is what makes the confrontation testable under Deuteronomy 18:22, where the mark of a word the LORD has not spoken is that the thing does not come to pass. A prophecy with a date on it can be checked; that is why Jeremiah answers as he does in 28:9 and lets the calendar decide.

translationNotes.term: Amen, may the LORD do so
translationNotes.note: Jeremiah's first reply in 28:6 is agreement with the wish. He is not pretending; he wanted the vessels and the exiles back too. He then separates what he would like from what has been said, which is why 28:8 appeals to the long line of prophets before them who prophesied war, famine and plague.

Hananiah's sign in 28:10 is to break the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and snap it. The reply in 28:13 accepts the act and raises it: you have broken wooden bars, and in their place there will be bars of iron. A wooden yoke can be split with an axe. An iron one cannot, which is the whole answer.

translationNotes.term: The seventh month of that same year
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 dates the confrontation to the fifth month; verse 17 records Hananiah's death in the seventh. Two months, exactly as 28:16 said, against the two years Hananiah had named. The book preserves both dates so the test can be checked.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hananiah prophesies that God will break Babylon's yoke within two years and restore the temple articles and exiles; Jeremiah counters that a prophet's truth is proved by whether his words come true, and after Hananiah symbolically breaks Jeremiah's wooden yoke, God tells Jeremiah to warn Hananiah he will die that year for preaching lies. Hananiah dies in the seventh month.

stories.title: 📨 Jeremiah 29
summaryBullets: This is the text of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders among the exiles and to the priests, the prophets, and all the others Nebuchadnezzar had carried into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. (29:1).
(This was after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the court officials, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metalsmiths had been exiled from Jerusalem.) (29:2).
The letter was entrusted to Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to King Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon. It stated: (29:3).
This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles who were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: (29:4).
“Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce. (29:5).
Take wives and have sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Multiply there; do not decrease. (29:6).
Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.” (29:7).
For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you, and do not listen to the dreams you elicit from them. (29:8).
For they are falsely prophesying to you in My name; I have not sent them, declares the LORD.” (29:9).
For this is what the LORD says: “When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place. (29:10).
For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope. (29:11).
Then you will call upon Me and come and pray to Me, and I will listen to you. (29:12).
You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart. (29:13).

I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore you from captivity and gather you from all the nations and places to which I have banished you, declares the LORD. I will restore you to the place from which I sent you into exile.” (29:14).
Because you may say, “The LORD has raised up for us prophets in Babylon,” (29:15).
this is what the LORD says about the king who sits on David’s throne and all the people who remain in this city, your brothers who did not go with you into exile— (29:16).
this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “I will send against them sword and famine and plague, and I will make them like rotten figs, so bad they cannot be eaten. (29:17).

I will pursue them with sword and famine and plague. I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth— a curse, a desolation, and an object of scorn and reproach among all the nations to which I banish them. (29:18).

I will do this because they have not listened to My words, declares the LORD,which I sent to them again and again through My servants the prophets. And neither have you exiles listened, declares the LORD.” (29:19).
So hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon. (29:20).

This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says about Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying to you lies in My name: “I will deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will kill them before your very eyes. (29:21).
Because of them, all the exiles of Judah who are in Babylon will use this curse: ‘May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire!’ (29:22).

For they have committed an outrage in Israel by committing adultery with the wives of their neighbors and speaking lies in My name, which I did not command them to do. I am He who knows, and I am a witness, declares the LORD.” (29:23).
You are to tell Shemaiah the Nehelamite that (29:24).

this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “In your own name you have sent out letters to all the people of Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, and to all the priests. You said to Zephaniah: (29:25).

‘The LORD has appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada, to be the chief officer in the house of the LORD, responsible for any madman who acts like a prophet — you must put him in stocks and neck irons. (29:26).
So now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who poses as a prophet among you? (29:27).
For he has sent to us in Babylon, claiming: Since the exile will be lengthy, build houses and settle down; plant gardens and eat their produce.’” (29:28).
(Zephaniah the priest, however, had read this letter to Jeremiah the prophet.) (29:29).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (29:30).

“Send a message telling all the exiles what the LORD says concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite. Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you— though I did not send him— and has made you trust in a lie, (29:31).

this is what the LORD says: ‘I will surely punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. He will have no one left among this people, nor will he see the good that I will bring to My people, declares the LORD, for he has preached rebellion against the LORD.’” (29:32).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 24:4-7: The vision of the good figs, the same exiles this letter is addressed to.
Daniel 1:3-7: Judean youths settled and trained in Babylon, life in the city Jeremiah tells the exiles to pray for.
Ezra 2:1-2: The list of those who came up out of the captivity, the return promised in 29:10-14.
Deuteronomy 4:29-30: You will seek the LORD and find Him when you search with all your heart, in the latter days.
1 Peter 2:11-12: Live honourably as sojourners among the nations, exile conduct in a later setting.

translationNotes.term: A letter carried by the king's envoys
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 names the couriers: Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, sent by Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar. A private citizen could not post a letter to Babylon; you needed the diplomatic bag. Jeremiah's letter travelled inside a Judean embassy, which is how it reached the exiles and how the reply in 29:25 came back.

Verses 5-6 tell the exiles to build, plant, marry, have children and marry those children off. Every instruction assumes decades. A garden takes seasons and an orchard longer, so the list is a way of saying the seventy years of 29:10 is real and they should stop living out of their bags.

translationNotes.term: Seek the welfare of the city
translationNotes.note: Shalom is not calm; it is soundness, safety, prosperity, the whole of a thing working. Verse 7 tells captives to work for the good of the empire that took them and to pray to the LORD for it, on the plain ground that their own welfare is inside its welfare.

The promise in 29:11 is spoken to a specific group at a specific time: the exiles of 597 BC, and 29:10 sets the term at seventy years first. Most of the people who first read the letter died in Babylon. The verse promises a future and a hope to the community, on the far side of a period longer than most of their lives.

Verse 22 records that Zedekiah son of Maaseiah and Ahab son of Kolaiah were burned to death by Nebuchadnezzar, and that their fate became a curse formula among the exiles. Execution by fire is attested in Babylonian practice and appears again in Daniel 3:6. The letter reports it as a thing that had already happened, not a threat.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah sends a letter to the exiles in Babylon instructing them to settle, build, marry, and seek the city's welfare, while warning them against false prophets; he also announces God's plan to restore them after seventy years and pronounces judgment against deceptive prophets like Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah.

stories.title: 🌄 Jeremiah 30
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: (30:1).
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. (30:2).

For behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah, declares the LORD. I will restore them to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they will possess it.’” (30:3).
These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah. (30:4).
Yes, this is what the LORD says: “A cry of panic is heard — a cry of terror, not of peace. (30:5).
Ask now, and see: Can a male give birth? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor and every face turned pale? (30:6).
How awful that day will be! None will be like it! It is the time of Jacob’s distress, but he will be saved out of it. (30:7).
On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will break the yoke off their necks and tear off their bonds, and no longer will strangers enslave them. (30:8).
Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them. (30:9).

As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, declares the LORD, and do not be dismayed, O Israel. For I will surely save you out of a distant place, your descendants from the land of their captivity! Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid. (30:10).

For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD. Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you. Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” (30:11).
For this is what the LORD says: “Your injury is incurable; your wound is grievous. (30:12).
There is no one to plead your cause, no remedy for your sores, no recovery for you. (30:13).

All your lovers have forgotten you; they no longer seek you, for I have struck you as an enemy would, with the discipline of someone cruel, because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins. (30:14).
Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain has no cure! Because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins I have done these things to you. (30:15).

Nevertheless, all who devour you will be devoured, and all your adversaries— every one of them— will go off into exile. Those who plundered you will be plundered, and all who raided you will be raided. (30:16).
But I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD, because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares.” (30:17).

This is what the LORD says: “I will restore the fortunes of Jacob’s tents and have compassion on his dwellings. And the city will be rebuilt on her own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place. (30:18).
Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration. I will multiply them, and they will not be decreased; I will honor them, and they will not be belittled. (30:19).
Their children will be as in days of old, and their congregation will be established before Me; and I will punish all their oppressors. (30:20).

Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst. And I will bring him near, and he will approach Me, for who would dare on his own to approach Me?” declares the LORD. (30:21).
“And you will be My people, and I will be your God.” (30:22).
Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked. (30:23).
The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart. In the days to come you will understand this. (30:24).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 30:1-5: When the curses have come and the people turn back, God restores their fortunes and gathers them.
Isaiah 1:5-6: The nation's wound described as untended bruises and open sores, the same diagnosis as 30:12-13.
Ezekiel 34:23-24: God sets one shepherd over them, His servant David, matching the ruler from their own midst in 30:21.
Daniel 12:1: A time of distress such as never was, out of which the people are delivered, matching 30:7.
Leviticus 26:40-45: Confession of iniquity and God remembering the covenant with their fathers, the turn 30:18-22 makes.

translationNotes.note: Verse 2 orders the words written down rather than only spoken. A scroll outlives the speaker and can be checked later against events, which is the point when the promise concerns a generation not yet born. Chapters 30 and 31 are often read together as the scroll that command produced.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵת־צָרָה הִיא לְיַעֲקֹב (eth tsarah hi le-Ya'aqov)
translationNotes.note: Verse 7 says the day is great, that none is like it, and that he will be saved out of it. The text sets no calendar date and gives no year. What it states is the severity and the outcome, in that order.

translationNotes.term: Hands on the loins like a woman in labour
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 asks why every strong man is standing with his hands pressed to his lower back, and every face has gone pale. The gesture is the one a woman in hard labour makes. Applied to soldiers, it is a picture of men doubled over in terror, and it is the standard prophetic image for a day of panic, used at 4:31, 6:24, 13:21 and 49:24.

Verses 12-15 use the language of a field surgeon: no one to plead the case, no medicine for the sore, no healing for the wound, no bandage. Verse 17 answers each item, I will restore your health and heal your wounds, so the second half of the chapter reads as a reply to its own diagnosis.

Verse 21 says the ruler will come from among them and be brought near, and asks who else would dare risk his life to approach. Access to God's presence was restricted; the high priest entered the innermost room once a year, and Leviticus 16:2 warns him not to come at any time he chooses. The line describes an approach freely made.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD commands Jeremiah to record his words of restoration: Israel and Judah will endure severe trouble but be saved from captivity, freed from foreign rule, and restored to their land with rebuilt cities and renewed prosperity. Though their enemies will be destroyed and their sins disciplined, God will heal their wounds and establish their leader from among them.

headings.text: The Restoration of Israel and Judah

stories.title: 🌄 Jeremiah 31
summaryBullets: “At that time,” declares the LORD, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be My people.” (31:1).
This is what the LORD says: “The people who survived the sword found favor in the wilderness when Israel went to find rest.” (31:2).
The LORD appeared to us in the past, saying: “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion. (31:3).
Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel. Again you will take up your tambourines and go out in joyful dancing. (31:4).
Again you will plant vineyards on the hills of Samaria; the farmers will plant and enjoy the fruit. (31:5).
For there will be a day when watchmen will call out on the hills of Ephraim, ‘Arise, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God!’” (31:6).
For this is what the LORD says: “Sing with joy for Jacob; shout for the foremost of the nations! Make your praises heard, and say, ‘O LORD, save Your people, the remnant of Israel!’ (31:7).

Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, including the blind and the lame, expectant mothers and women in labor. They will return as a great assembly! (31:8).

They will come with weeping, and by their supplication I will lead them; I will make them walk beside streams of waters, on a level path where they will not stumble. For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn.” (31:9).
Hear, O nations, the word of the LORD, and proclaim it in distant coastlands: “The One who scattered Israel will gather them and keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock. (31:10).
For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and redeemed him from the hand that had overpowered him. (31:11).

They will come and shout for joy on the heights of Zion; they will be radiant over the bounty of the LORD — the grain, new wine, and oil, and the young of the flocks and herds. Their life will be like a well-watered garden, and never again will they languish. (31:12).
Then the maidens will rejoice with dancing, young men and old as well. I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow. (31:13).
I will fill the souls of the priests abundantly, and will fill My people with My goodness,” declares the LORD. (31:14).
This is what the LORD says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.” (31:15).

This is what the LORD says: “Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for the reward for your work will come, declares the LORD. Then your children will return from the land of the enemy. (31:16).
So there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children will return to their own land. (31:17).
I have surely heard Ephraim’s moaning: ‘You disciplined me severely, like an untrained calf. Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God. (31:18).
After I returned, I repented; and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh in grief. I was ashamed and humiliated because I bore the disgrace of my youth.’ (31:19).

Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child? Though I often speak against him, I still remember him. Therefore My heart yearns for him; I have great compassion for him,” declares the LORD. (31:20).
“Set up the road markers, put up the signposts. Keep the highway in mind, the road you have traveled. Return, O Virgin Israel, return to these cities of yours. (31:21).
How long will you wander, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing in the land— a woman will shelter a man.” (31:22).

This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “When I restore them from captivity, they will once again speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities: ‘May the LORD bless you, O righteous dwelling place, O holy mountain.’ (31:23).
And Judah and all its cities will dwell together in the land, the farmers and those who move with the flocks, (31:24).
for I will refresh the weary soul and replenish all who are weak.” (31:25).
At this I awoke and looked around. My sleep had been most pleasant to me. (31:26).
“The days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and of beast. (31:27).
Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down, to demolish, destroy, and bring disaster, so I will watch over them to build and to plant,” declares the LORD. (31:28).
“In those days, it will no longer be said: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge.’ (31:29).
Instead, each will die for his own iniquity. If anyone eats the sour grapes, his own teeth will be set on edge. (31:30).
Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. (31:31).

It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt— a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD. (31:32).

“But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. (31:33).

No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” (31:34).
Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day, who sets in order the moon and stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar — the LORD of Hosts is His name: (31:35).
“Only if this fixed order departed from My presence, declares the LORD, would Israel’s descendants ever cease to be a nation before Me.” (31:36).

This is what the LORD says: “Only if the heavens above could be measured and the foundations of the earth below searched out would I reject all of Israel’s descendants because of all they have done,” declares the LORD. (31:37).
“The days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when this city will be rebuilt for Me, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. (31:38).
The measuring line will once again stretch out straight to the hill of Gareb and then turn toward Goah. (31:39).

The whole valley of the dead bodies and ashes, and all the fields as far as the Kidron Valley, to the corner of the Horse Gate to the east, will be holy to the LORD. It will never again be uprooted or demolished.” (31:40).
crossRefs: Hebrews 8:8-12: The new covenant of 31:31-34 quoted in full and applied.
Hebrews 10:16-17: The same passage quoted a second time, for laws on the heart and sins remembered no more.
Matthew 2:16-18: Rachel weeping for her children applied when Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem.
Genesis 35:16-20: Rachel dies in childbirth and is buried on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem, the grave 31:15 speaks from.
Ezekiel 36:26-27: A new heart and God's Spirit put within His people, the same promise in different words.

translationNotes.note: Jacob's wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, buried on the road near Bethlehem according to Genesis 35:19. Ramah in 31:15 is a town in Benjamin about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem, and 40:1 records it as the staging camp where prisoners were chained before the march to Babylon. The verse puts the mother of the northern tribes at a deportation depot, hearing her descendants pass.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה (berith chadashah) - Greek: διαθήκη καινή (diatheke kaine)
translationNotes.note: Verses 31-34 are the only place in the Old Testament where the phrase new covenant appears. Four things are named: God's instruction written on the heart rather than on stone, the relationship formula I will be their God and they will be My people, everyone knowing Him without needing to be taught, and sins forgiven and not remembered. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes the whole passage.

Verse 21 tells the exiles going out to plant markers and guideposts along the way, and to note the highway they are travelling. Caravan routes were marked with cairns and pillars so a traveller could find the road back across country with no landmarks. The instruction assumes the return trip before the outward journey is finished.

Verse 29 quotes a saying doing the rounds in Judah: the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. It is a complaint about inherited punishment. Verse 30 cancels it, and Ezekiel 18:1-4 takes the same saying and answers it at chapter length.

translationNotes.term: The fixed order of sun, moon and stars
translationNotes.note: Verses 35-37 stake the promise on two things nobody can move: the daily and nightly order of the lights, and the unmeasured size of the heavens and the foundations of the earth. The argument is a wager. If the first can be broken, the second falls too.

translationNotes.term: The valley of the dead bodies and the ashes
translationNotes.note: Verse 40 names the Hinnom ravine and the ash dumps south of Jerusalem, the ground where children had been burned at Topheth in 7:31 and 19:5. The chapter ends by declaring that ground holy to the LORD and inside the rebuilt city.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD promises to restore Israel from exile, gathering them from distant lands and establishing a new covenant where his law is written on their hearts and all people know him directly; Jerusalem will be rebuilt and made holy.

stories.title: 🧾 Jeremiah 32
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. (32:1).
At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, which was in the palace of the king of Judah. (32:2).

For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying: “Why are you prophesying like this? You claim that the LORD says, ‘Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it. (32:3).

Zedekiah king of Judah will not escape from the hands of the Chaldeans, but he will surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and will speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. (32:4).
He will take Zedekiah to Babylon, where he will stay until I attend to him, declares the LORD. If you fight against the Chaldeans, you will not succeed.’” (32:5).
Jeremiah replied, “The word of the LORD came to me, saying: (32:6).
Behold! Hanamel, the son of your uncle Shallum, is coming to you to say, ‘Buy for yourself my field in Anathoth, for you have the right of redemption to buy it.’ (32:7).

Then, as the LORD had said, my cousin Hanamel came to me in the courtyard of the guard and urged me, ‘Please buy my field in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for you own the right of inheritance and redemption. Buy it for yourself.’” Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD. (32:8).
So I bought the field in Anathoth from my cousin Hanamel, and I weighed out seventeen shekels of silver. (32:9).
I signed and sealed the deed, called in witnesses, and weighed out the silver on the scales. (32:10).
Then I took the deed of purchase— the sealed copy with its terms and conditions, as well as the open copy— (32:11).

and I gave this deed to Baruch son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the sight of my cousin Hanamel and the witnesses who were signing the purchase agreement and all the Jews sitting in the courtyard of the guard. (32:12).
In their sight I instructed Baruch, (32:13).

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Take these deeds— both the sealed copy and the open copy of the deed of purchase— and put them in a clay jar to preserve them for a long time. (32:14).
For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.” (32:15).
After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD: (32:16).
“Oh, Lord GOD! You have made the heavens and the earth by Your great power and outstretched arm. Nothing is too difficult for You! (32:17).
You show loving devotion to thousands but lay the iniquity of the fathers into the laps of their children after them, O great and mighty God whose name is the LORD of Hosts, (32:18).
the One great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are on all the ways of the sons of men, to reward each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds. (32:19).
You performed signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and You do so to this very day, both in Israel and among all mankind. And You have made a name for Yourself, as is the case to this day. (32:20).
You brought Your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with great terror. (32:21).
You gave them this land that You had sworn to give their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey. (32:22).

They came in and possessed it, but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law. They failed to perform all that You commanded them to do, and so You have brought upon them all this disaster. (32:23).

See how the siege ramps are mounted against the city to capture it. And by sword and famine and plague, the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What You have spoken has happened, as You now see! (32:24).
Yet You, O Lord GOD, have said to me, ‘Buy for yourself the field with silver and call in witnesses, even though the city has been delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans!’” (32:25).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (32:26).
“Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too difficult for Me? (32:27).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will capture it. (32:28).

And the Chaldeans who are fighting against this city will come in, set it on fire, and burn it, along with the houses of those who provoked Me to anger by burning incense to Baal on their rooftops and by pouring out drink offerings to other gods. (32:29).

For the children of Israel and of Judah have done nothing but evil in My sight from their youth; indeed, they have done nothing but provoke Me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD. (32:30).
For this city has aroused My wrath and fury from the day it was built until now. Therefore I will remove it from My presence (32:31).

because of all the evil the children of Israel and of Judah have done to provoke Me to anger— they, their kings, their officials, their priests and prophets, the men of Judah, and the residents of Jerusalem. (32:32).
They have turned their backs to Me and not their faces. Though I taught them again and again, they would not listen or respond to discipline. (32:33).
They have placed their abominations in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it. (32:34).

They have built the high places of Baal in the Valley of Ben-hinnom to make their sons and daughters pass through the fire to Molech— something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind, that they should commit such an abomination and cause Judah to sin. (32:35).
Now therefore, about this city of which you say, ‘It will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword and famine and plague,’ this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: (32:36).
I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them in My furious anger and great wrath, and I will return them to this place and make them dwell in safety. (32:37).
They will be My people, and I will be their God. (32:38).
I will give them one heart and one way, so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them. (32:39).
I will make an everlasting covenant with them: I will never turn away from doing good to them, and I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me. (32:40).
Yes , I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will faithfully plant them in this land with all My heart and with all My soul. (32:41).
For this is what the LORD says: Just as I have brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring on them all the good I have promised them. (32:42).
And fields will be bought in this land about which you are saying, ‘It is a desolation, without man or beast; it has been delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans.’ (32:43).

Fields will be purchased with silver, and deeds will be signed, sealed, and witnessed in the land of Benjamin, in the areas surrounding Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah— the cities of the hill country, the foothills, and the Negev— because I will restore them from captivity, declares the LORD.” (32:44).
crossRefs: Leviticus 25:23-28: The redemption law giving the nearest kinsman first claim to buy family land, the right Hanamel brings in 32:7-8.
Ruth 4:1-11: A land redemption transacted at the gate before elders and witnesses, with the terms said out loud.
Genesis 18:14: Is anything too hard for the LORD, the question Jeremiah asks in 32:17 and God returns in 32:27.
Jeremiah 39:1-10: The siege and the fall of the city that this purchase is made during.
Jeremiah 7:31: Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom named again in 32:35 as a thing God never commanded.

translationNotes.term: The sealed deed and the open copy
translationNotes.note: This is real Judean conveyancing, set out step by step in 32:9-14. The terms were written out twice on one sheet. The upper text was rolled, tied and sealed with the witnesses' seal impressions so it could not be altered; the lower text was left open for anyone to read. Only a court could break the seal, and then the two copies were compared. Double documents of exactly this form survive from Jewish communities at Elephantine in Egypt and from caves in the Judean desert.

Verse 10 says he weighed the silver, because there were no coins in Judah in 587 BC. Silver moved as cut pieces and ingots measured on a balance against stone weights, and Judean weights inscribed with the shekel mark have been recovered by the hundred. Coinage reached Judah only under the Persians, more than a century later. The Hebrew word shekel is the verb to weigh.

A shekel weighed about two fifths of an ounce (11.4 grams), so seventeen shekels is roughly seven ounces (194 grams) of silver. For scale, Judges 17:10 has a Levite hired for ten shekels a year plus clothing and board, and Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as the compensation for a slave killed by an ox. It is a real price for a field, paid for land the Babylonian army was standing on.

Leviticus 25:23-28 forbids selling family land off permanently, on the ground that the land belongs to God and Israelites are tenants on it. When a man had to sell, the nearest kinsman had first claim to buy it in and keep it in the clan. Hanamel comes to Jeremiah in 32:7-8 because Jeremiah is that kinsman; the purchase is a legal duty, not a speculation.

translationNotes.term: A clay jar to preserve them
translationNotes.note: Verse 14 puts both copies in an earthenware jar. Sealed pottery keeps papyrus and leather dry and away from insects for a very long time, which is exactly how the Dead Sea scrolls survived. The instruction says the deed has to last long enough to be produced by an heir, which is the point of the whole transaction.

stories.keyTakeaway: While Jerusalem is under siege and Jeremiah is imprisoned, he buys a field from his cousin as instructed by God, then prays in confusion before God assures him that despite the coming destruction, he will restore the people and prosperity to the land.

stories.title: 🧾 Jeremiah 33
summaryBullets: While Jeremiah was still confined in the courtyard of the guard, the word of the LORD came to him a second time: (33:1).
“Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it and established it, the LORD is His name: (33:2).
Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know. (33:3).

For this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the houses of this city and the palaces of the kings of Judah that have been torn down for defense against the siege ramps and the sword: (33:4).

The Chaldeans are coming to fight and to fill those places with the corpses of the men I will strike down in My anger and in My wrath. I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness. (33:5).
Nevertheless, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people and reveal to them the abundance of peace and truth. (33:6).
I will restore Judah and Israel from captivity and will rebuild them as in former times. (33:7).
And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me. (33:8).

So this city will bring Me renown, joy, praise, and glory before all the nations of the earth, who will hear of all the good I do for it. They will tremble in awe because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it. (33:9).

This is what the LORD says: In this place you say is a wasteland without man or beast, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem that are deserted — inhabited by neither man nor beast — there will be heard again (33:10).

the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, and the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD, saying: ‘Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever.’ For I will restore the land from captivity as in former times, says the LORD. (33:11).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: In this desolate place, without man or beast, and in all its cities, there will once more be pastures for shepherds to rest their flocks. (33:12).

In the cities of the hill country, the foothills, and the Negev, in the land of Benjamin and the cities surrounding Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, the flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD. (33:13).
Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the gracious promise that I have spoken to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. (33:14).
In those days and at that time I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch, and He will administer justice and righteousness in the land. (33:15).
In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness. (33:16).
For this is what the LORD says: David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel, (33:17).
nor will the priests who are Levites ever fail to have a man before Me to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices.” (33:18).
And the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (33:19).
“This is what the LORD says: If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night, so that day and night cease to occupy their appointed time, (33:20).
then My covenant may also be broken with David My servant and with My ministers the Levites who are priests, so that David will not have a son to reign on his throne. (33:21).

As the hosts of heaven cannot be counted and as the sand on the seashore cannot be measured, so too will I multiply the descendants of My servant David and the Levites who minister before Me.” (33:22).
Moreover, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (33:23).
“Have you not noticed what these people are saying: ‘The LORD has rejected the two families He had chosen’? So they despise My people and no longer regard them as a nation. (33:24).
This is what the LORD says: If I have not established My covenant with the day and the night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, (33:25).

then I would also reject the descendants of Jacob and of My servant David, so as not to take from his descendants rulers over the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them.” (33:26).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 23:5-6: The Righteous Branch promised earlier, with the same title given to the king.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The oath to David that his house, kingdom and throne will be established forever.
Genesis 8:22: Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, day and night will not cease, the covenant 33:20-21 appeals to.
Numbers 25:12-13: A covenant of perpetual priesthood given to Phinehas and his descendants after him.
Luke 1:32-33: Gabriel tells Mary that her son will be given the throne of His father David and will reign forever.

translationNotes.term: Still shut in the court of the guard
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 notes that this word came while Jeremiah was still confined, which ties it to the siege of chapter 32. The court of the guard was an open yard attached to the palace where a prisoner could receive visitors and transact business, which is how the land purchase of 32:6-15 happened at all. It was not a cell.

The word in 33:3 is the one used for a fortified city with high walls, so the sense is things walled off and out of reach. It is the same root that gives fortified cities in 4:5 and 34:7. Verse 3 offers access to matters that are otherwise closed.

translationNotes.term: Houses torn down for the siege
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 records that houses in Jerusalem, including royal ones, were being demolished. Defenders pulled down buildings for stone and timber to plug breaches and raise the wall against a Babylonian ramp, and the cleared ground denied the attackers cover. It is a detail from inside a city fighting for its life.

translationNotes.term: As countless as the stars and the sand
translationNotes.note: Verse 22 puts the promise to David and to the Levites in the wording of the promise to Abraham in Genesis 22:17. Multiplying priests and kings by that formula is a deliberate borrowing, and 33:25-26 then names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to close the loop.

translationNotes.term: The two families the LORD chose
translationNotes.note: Verse 24 quotes what people were saying: that God had rejected the two families He chose. The two are Israel and Judah, split since 931 BC, or on another reading the line of David and the line of Levi that 33:17-18 has just named. Either way the complaint is that the election is over, and 33:25-26 answers it with the fixed order of day and night.

stories.keyTakeaway: God promises Jeremiah that despite the destruction Jerusalem faces, he will heal the land, restore Judah and Israel from captivity, and establish a righteous descendant of David to rule; God's covenant with David and the Levitical priests will endure as surely as day and night.

headings.text: The Excellence of the Restored Nation

stories.title: 🏚️ Jeremiah 34
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, all his army, all the earthly kingdoms under his control, and all the other nations were fighting against Jerusalem and all its surrounding cities. (34:1).

The LORD, the God of Israel, told Jeremiah to go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and tell him that this is what the LORD says: “Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it down. (34:2).

And you yourself will not escape his grasp, but will surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You will see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face; and you will go to Babylon. (34:3).
Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah. This is what the LORD says concerning you: You will not die by the sword; (34:4).

you will die in peace. As spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who preceded you, so people will burn spices for you and lament, ‘Alas, O master!’ For I Myself have spoken this word, declares the LORD.” (34:5).
In Jerusalem, then, Jeremiah the prophet relayed all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah (34:6).
as the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah— against Lachish and Azekah. For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah. (34:7).
After King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty, the word came to Jeremiah from the LORD (34:8).
that each man should free his Hebrew slaves, both male and female, and no one should hold his fellow Jew in bondage. (34:9).

So all the officials and all the people who entered into this covenant agreed that they would free their menservants and maidservants and no longer hold them in bondage. They obeyed and released them, (34:10).
but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed, and they forced them to become slaves again. (34:11).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying, (34:12).
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I made a covenant with your forefathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying: (34:13).

Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother who has sold himself to you. He may serve you six years, but then you must let him go free. But your fathers did not listen or incline their ear. (34:14).
Recently you repented and did what pleased Me; each of you proclaimed freedom for his neighbor. You made a covenant before Me in the house that bears My Name. (34:15).

But now you have changed your minds and profaned My name. Each of you has taken back the menservants and maidservants whom you had set at liberty to go wherever they wanted, and you have again forced them to be your slaves. (34:16).

Therefore this is what the LORD says: You have not obeyed Me; you have not proclaimed freedom, each man for his brother and for his neighbor. So now I proclaim freedom for you, declares the LORD — freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine! I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. (34:17).

And those who have transgressed My covenant and have not fulfilled the terms of the covenant they made before Me, I will treat like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces. (34:18).
The officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the pieces of the calf, (34:19).
I will deliver into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives. Their corpses will become food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. (34:20).
And I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives, to the army of the king of Babylon that had withdrawn from you. (34:21).

Behold, I am going to give the command, declares the LORD, and I will bring them back to this city. They will fight against it, capture it, and burn it down. And I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.” (34:22).
crossRefs: Exodus 21:2-6: A Hebrew slave serves six years and goes free in the seventh, the law 34:14 cites.
Deuteronomy 15:12-18: The same release law, with the added command not to send him away empty-handed.
Leviticus 25:39-43: An Israelite in debt is not to be worked as a slave but as a hired man, and goes free at the Jubilee.
Genesis 15:9-18: Animals cut in two and a flame passing between the pieces, the oath ritual behind 34:18-20.
2 Kings 25:1-7: The siege, the night flight and Zedekiah's capture, the end 34:2-5 announces.

translationNotes.note: Hebrew does not make a covenant, it cuts one, and 34:18 shows why. The parties cut an animal in two and walked between the halves. The unspoken sentence was let this be done to me if I break my word, which is why God says the men who passed between the calf's pieces and then broke the oath will be handed over and become food for birds.

Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 require a Hebrew bought as a slave to be freed after six years of service. Verse 14 says the fathers did not listen and the law had been ignored for generations. Under siege the owners suddenly kept it, and 34:11 records that as soon as the Babylonian army withdrew they took their freed people back. The word deror is the same one used for the Jubilee proclamation in Leviticus 25:10.

Verse 7 says these two were the last fortified cities of Judah still holding out besides Jerusalem. Lachish guarded the approach from the coastal plain about twenty-five miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem; Azekah sat between them in the Elah valley. A group of inscribed potsherds found in the gate of Lachish, written during this war, includes a soldier reporting that he is watching for the fire signals of Lachish because he can no longer see Azekah.

Verse 5 promises Zedekiah death in peace with the customary funeral fire and the lament Alas, lord. It is not a promise of escape. 39:7 and 52:11 record that he was blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze fetters, and 52:11 adds that he stayed in prison there until the day of his death, dying a captive rather than by the sword.

translationNotes.term: Spices burned at a royal funeral
translationNotes.note: The burning promised in 34:5 is not cremation, which Israel did not practise. It is a fire of aromatics kindled in the king's honour, recorded for Asa in 2 Chronicles 16:14 and denied to Jehoram in 2 Chronicles 21:19. Withholding it was an insult; granting it, as here, is the promise of a proper burial.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Babylon will capture Jerusalem and burn it, though Zedekiah himself will die peacefully; later, God condemns the people for freeing their Hebrew slaves and then re-enslaving them, promising them death by sword, plague, and famine instead.

stories.title: 🏚️ Jeremiah 35
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah: (35:1).
“Go to the house of the Rechabites, speak to them, and bring them to one of the chambers of the house of the LORD to offer them a drink of wine.” (35:2).
So I took Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah, the son of Habazziniah, and his brothers and all his sons— the entire house of the Rechabites— (35:3).

and I brought them into the house of the LORD, to a chamber occupied by the sons of Hanan son of Igdaliah, a man of God. This room was near the chamber of the officials, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah son of Shallum the doorkeeper. (35:4).
Then I set pitchers full of wine and some cups before the men of the house of the Rechabites, and I said to them, “Drink some wine.” (35:5).
“We do not drink wine,” they replied, “for our forefather Jonadab son of Rechab commanded us, ‘Neither you nor your descendants are ever to drink wine. (35:6).

Nor are you ever to build a house or sow seed or plant a vineyard. Those things are not for you. Instead, you must live in tents all your lives, so that you may live a long time in the land where you wander.’ (35:7).
And we have obeyed the voice of our forefather Jonadab son of Rechab in all he commanded us. So we have not drunk wine all our lives— neither we nor our wives nor our sons and daughters. (35:8).
Nor have we built houses in which to live, and we have not owned any vineyards or fields or crops. (35:9).
But we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done exactly as our forefather Jonadab commanded us. (35:10).

So when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched into the land, we said: ‘Come, let us go into Jerusalem to escape the armies of the Chaldeans and the Arameans.’ So we have remained in Jerusalem.” (35:11).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (35:12).
“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Go and tell the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem: ‘Will you not accept discipline and obey My words?’ declares the LORD. (35:13).

The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out. He commanded his sons not to drink wine, and they have not drunk it to this very day because they have obeyed the command of their forefather. But I have spoken to you again and again, and you have not obeyed Me! (35:14).

Again and again I have sent you all My servants the prophets, proclaiming: ‘Turn now, each of you, from your wicked ways, and correct your actions. Do not go after other gods to serve them. Live in the land that I have given to you and your fathers.’ But you have not inclined your ear or listened to Me. (35:15).
Yes, the sons of Jonadab son of Rechab carried out the command their forefather gave them, but these people have not listened to Me. (35:16).

Therefore this is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will bring to Judah and to all the residents of Jerusalem all the disaster I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them but they have not obeyed, and I have called to them but they have not answered.’” (35:17).

Then Jeremiah said to the house of the Rechabites: “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Because you have obeyed the command of your forefather Jonadab and have kept all his commandments and have done all that he charged you to do, (35:18).
this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Jonadab son of Rechab will never fail to have a man to stand before Me.’” (35:19).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 10:15-23: Jehonadab son of Rechab rides with Jehu into Samaria and helps wipe out the worship of Baal.
1 Chronicles 2:55: The Rechabites listed among the scribal families of Kenite descent.
Numbers 6:1-4: The Nazirite vow, the other Israelite abstention from wine and everything from the vine.
Exodus 20:12: Honour your father and mother, the commandment the Rechabites keep and Judah does not.
Jeremiah 7:25-26: God sending His servants the prophets again and again since the exodus, the same complaint repeated in 35:15.

translationNotes.note: A clan living inside Judah under a rule laid down by their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab, set out in their own words in 35:6-7: no wine, no house, no sowing, no vineyard, live in tents. That is a deliberate refusal of settled agriculture, which is the whole economy of Canaan and the whole culture of its fertility worship. They had kept it for well over two centuries by the time Jeremiah tests them.

A real figure with a dated appearance elsewhere. 2 Kings 10:15-23 has Jehu pull him up into his chariot and take him into the temple of Baal in Samaria to help clear it out, about 841 BC. That places the founding of the Rechabite rule some two and a half centuries before this chapter.

translationNotes.term: Set before them pitchers of wine
translationNotes.note: Verses 2-5 are staged. Jeremiah brings the clan into a chamber of the temple itself, sets out full jars and cups, and tells them to drink, using the authority of the place and the prophet at once. The refusal in 35:6 is made against maximum pressure, which is what makes it usable as evidence in 35:14.

translationNotes.term: Chambers of the house of the LORD
translationNotes.note: Rooms built into the temple courts and used for stores, for meals from the offerings, and by officials and prominent families. Verse 4 names the room used as the one belonging to the sons of Hanan, next to the officials' chamber and above the room of the doorkeeper Maaseiah, which is precise enough to locate the scene for anyone who knew the building.

translationNotes.term: Will never fail to have a man to stand before Me
translationNotes.note: The promise in 35:19 uses the phrase for permanent service in God's presence, the same idiom applied to the Levites in 33:18 and to David's line in 33:17. It is granted here to a clan that was not Israelite by descent; 1 Chronicles 2:55 traces the Rechabites to the Kenites, the people of Moses' father-in-law.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah brings the Rekabites wine to test their obedience; they refuse because their ancestor Jehonadab commanded them never to drink wine, and God uses their faithfulness to contrast Judah's persistent disobedience to his prophets, pronouncing judgment on Jerusalem while blessing the Rekabite line.

stories.title: 🏚️ Jeremiah 36
summaryBullets: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: (36:1).
“Take a scroll and write on it all the words I have spoken to you concerning Israel, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I first spoke to you during the reign of Josiah until today. (36:2).
Perhaps when the people of Judah hear about all the calamity I plan to bring upon them, each of them will turn from his wicked way. Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.” (36:3).
So Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and at the dictation of Jeremiah, Baruch wrote on a scroll all the words that the LORD had spoken to Jeremiah. (36:4).
Then Jeremiah commanded Baruch, “I am restricted; I cannot enter the house of the LORD; (36:5).

so you are to go to the house of the LORD on a day of fasting, and in the hearing of the people you are to read the words of the LORD from the scroll you have written at my dictation. Read them in the hearing of all the people of Judah who are coming from their cities. (36:6).
Perhaps they will bring their petition before the LORD, and each one will turn from his wicked way; for great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced against this people.” (36:7).
So Baruch son of Neriah did everything that Jeremiah the prophet had commanded him. In the house of the LORD he read the words of the LORD from the scroll. (36:8).

Now in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, a fast before the LORD was proclaimed to all the people of Jerusalem and all who had come there from the cities of Judah. (36:9).

From the chamber of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, which was in the upper courtyard at the opening of the New Gate of the house of the LORD, Baruch read from the scroll the words of Jeremiah in the hearing of all the people. (36:10).
When Micaiah son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll, (36:11).

he went down to the scribe’s chamber in the king’s palace, where all the officials were sitting: Elishama the scribe, Delaiah son of Shemaiah, Elnathan son of Achbor, Gemariah son of Shaphan, Zedekiah son of Hananiah, and all the other officials. (36:12).
And Micaiah reported to them all the words he had heard Baruch read from the scroll in the hearing of the people. (36:13).

Then all the officials sent word to Baruch through Jehudi son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, saying, “Bring the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come here.” So Baruch son of Neriah took the scroll and went to them. (36:14).
“Please sit down,” they said, “and read it in our hearing.” So Baruch read it in their hearing. (36:15).
When they had heard all these words, they turned to one another in fear and said to Baruch, “Surely we must report all these words to the king.” (36:16).
“Tell us now,” they asked Baruch, “how did you write all these words? Was it at Jeremiah’s dictation?” (36:17).
“It was at his dictation,” Baruch replied. “He recited all these words to me and I wrote them in ink on the scroll.” (36:18).
Then the officials said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah must hide yourselves and tell no one where you are.” (36:19).
So the officials went to the king in the courtyard. And having stored the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, they reported everything to the king. (36:20).

Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the scribe. And Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king and all the officials who were standing beside him. (36:21).
Since it was the ninth month, the king was sitting in his winter quarters with a fire burning before him. (36:22).

And as soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns, Jehoiakim would cut them off with a scribe’s knife and throw them into the firepot, until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire. (36:23).
Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments. (36:24).
Even though Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them. (36:25).

Instead, the king commanded Jerahmeel, a son of the king, as well as Seraiah son of Azriel and Shelemiah son of Abdeel, to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. But the LORD had hidden them. (36:26).
After the king had burned the scroll containing the words that Baruch had written at Jeremiah’s dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: (36:27).
“Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned. (36:28).

You are to proclaim concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah that this is what the LORD says: You have burned the scroll and said, ‘Why have you written on it that the king of Babylon would surely come and destroy this land and deprive it of man and beast?’ (36:29).

Therefore this is what the LORD says about Jehoiakim king of Judah: He will have no one to sit on David’s throne, and his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night. (36:30).

I will punish him and his descendants and servants for their iniquity. I will bring on them, on the residents of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the calamity about which I warned them but they did not listen.” (36:31).

Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah, and at Jeremiah’s dictation he wrote on it all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them. (36:32).
crossRefs: Exodus 24:4-7: Moses writes down the words of the LORD and reads them aloud in the hearing of the people.
2 Kings 22:8-13: The book of the law found in the temple and read to Josiah, who tears his clothes; his son does not.
Deuteronomy 31:9-13: The law written out and read aloud to the whole assembly every seventh year.
Jeremiah 45:1-5: The word spoken to Baruch, dated to the same year in which he wrote this scroll.
Jeremiah 22:18-19: The burial denied to Jehoiakim, the sentence repeated in 36:30.

translationNotes.note: Baruch's trade was a physical craft. He wrote with a reed cut to a chisel tip and split, dipped in carbon ink made from lamp soot bound with gum and water, on sheets of papyrus glued edge to edge into a roll or on prepared skins sewn together. He carried a knife to trim the reed and the sheet, and a palette or inkhorn at his belt of the kind Ezekiel 9:2 describes. Ink of this sort sits on the surface and can be sponged off wet, which is why 36:18 stresses that he wrote with ink.

The word in 36:23 literally means doors. A scroll was written in vertical columns side by side along the roll, and the reader unwound with one hand and wound with the other, so the columns swung past like a row of doors. Jehudi read three or four of them at a time, which is how far you would unroll before pausing.

A small blade from the scribe's own kit, used to cut sheets and to trim reed pens. Verse 23 has the king using a scribe's own tool to destroy a scribe's work, slicing off each read column and dropping it into the brazier until the whole roll was gone. It is a slow, deliberate act, not a single throw into the fire.

translationNotes.term: The winter house and the firepot
translationNotes.note: Judean palaces had separate summer and winter quarters; the winter rooms faced the sun and were smaller and easier to heat. Verse 22 fixes the season by the ninth month, roughly December, with a charcoal brazier burning in front of the king. The detail is what makes the fire available in the room.

translationNotes.term: A fast in the ninth month
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 dates the reading to a public fast proclaimed for everyone in Jerusalem and everyone who had come in from the towns of Judah, in the fifth year of Jehoiakim, about 604 BC.
