That is the year Babylon sacked the Philistine city of Ashkelon. A fast filled the temple courts, which is why Baruch was told to read on that day.

translationNotes.term: Another scroll with many similar words added
translationNotes.note: Verse 32 says the whole text was dictated again to Baruch and that many similar words were added to it. The book records its own second edition, which is the clearest statement in the Old Testament of how a prophetic scroll came together.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jeremiah dictates his prophecies to Baruch, who reads them at the temple; officials hear the words and warn Jeremiah to hide, but King Jehoiakim burns the scroll and orders their arrest. God then commands Jeremiah to write the words again on another scroll, with additional words, and pronounces judgment against the king.

headings.text: Jeremiah’s Scroll Read in the Temple
Jeremiah’s Scroll Read in the Palace

stories.title: 🕳️ Jeremiah 37
summaryBullets: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made Zedekiah son of Josiah the king of Judah, and he reigned in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim. (37:1).
But he and his officers and the people of the land refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet. (37:2).
Yet King Zedekiah sent Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet with the message, “Please pray to the LORD our God for us!” (37:3).
Now Jeremiah was free to come and go among the people, for they had not yet put him in prison. (37:4).
Pharaoh’s army had left Egypt, and when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard the report, they withdrew from Jerusalem. (37:5).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: (37:6).

“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says that you are to tell the king of Judah, who sent you to Me: Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which has marched out to help you, will go back to its own land of Egypt. (37:7).
Then the Chaldeans will return and fight against this city. They will capture it and burn it down. (37:8).
This is what the LORD says: Do not deceive yourselves by saying, ‘The Chaldeans will go away for good,’ for they will not! (37:9).

Indeed, if you were to strike down the entire army of the Chaldeans that is fighting against you, and only wounded men remained in their tents, they would still get up and burn this city down.” (37:10).
When the Chaldean army withdrew from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh’s army, (37:11).
Jeremiah started to leave Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to claim his portion there among the people. (37:12).
But when he reached the Gate of Benjamin, the captain of the guard, whose name was Irijah son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah, seized him and said, “You are deserting to the Chaldeans!” (37:13).
“That is a lie,” Jeremiah replied. “I am not deserting to the Chaldeans!” But Irijah would not listen to him; instead, he arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials. (37:14).
The officials were angry with Jeremiah, and they beat him and placed him in jail in the house of Jonathan the scribe, for it had been made into a prison. (37:15).
So Jeremiah went into a cell in the dungeon and remained there a long time. (37:16).

Later, King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah and received him in his palace, where he asked him privately, “Is there a word from the LORD?” “There is,” Jeremiah replied. “You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.” (37:17).
Then Jeremiah asked King Zedekiah, “How have I sinned against you or your servants or these people, that you have put me in prison? (37:18).
Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, claiming, ‘The king of Babylon will not come against you or this land’ ? (37:19).
But now please listen, O my lord the king. May my petition come before you. Do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, or I will die there.” (37:20).

So King Zedekiah gave orders for Jeremiah to be placed in the courtyard of the guard and given a loaf of bread daily from the street of the bakers, until all the bread in the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard. (37:21).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:1-2: Zedekiah's rebellion and the start of the siege of Jerusalem, the situation this chapter sits inside.
Ezekiel 17:15-18: Zedekiah's appeal to Egypt for horses and troops named as a broken oath to Babylon.
Jeremiah 34:21-22: The Babylonian army withdrawing and then returning to burn the city, the lull described in 37:5-11.
Jeremiah 21:1-2: Zedekiah's earlier inquiry through the same priest Zephaniah, and the same answer.
Lamentations 4:17: Eyes worn out watching for a nation that could not save, the failed Egyptian relief.

translationNotes.term: Pharaoh's army came out of Egypt
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 records a relief force under Pharaoh Hophra, called Apries in Greek sources, marching up from Egypt in 588 BC. The Babylonians lifted the siege to meet it. Jerusalem read the withdrawal as deliverance, and 37:8 tells them the Egyptians will go home and the Chaldeans will come back and burn the city, which is what happened.

The people of the marshlands of southern Mesopotamia who took the Babylonian throne under Nabopolassar in 626 BC. Jeremiah uses Chaldeans and Babylonians for the same army throughout the book. In Daniel 2:2 the word also covers a class of court diviners, which is a later and narrower use.

The northern gate of Jerusalem, on the road toward Anathoth. Verse 12 says Jeremiah was leaving during the Babylonian withdrawal to take possession of property among his people, which fits the land transaction of chapter 32. The sentry's charge in 37:13, that he was deserting to the Chaldeans, was plausible precisely because Jeremiah had been publicly telling people to do exactly that in 21:9.

Verse 16 puts him in a vaulted cellar and its cells, in a private house converted to a prison. Hebrew calls it the house of the pit; underground storage chambers cut for grain or water were the ordinary way to hold a prisoner, since Judah had no purpose-built jails. Verse 20 is Jeremiah asking not to be sent back there because he would die in it.

translationNotes.term: A loaf of bread daily from the bakers' street
translationNotes.note: Verse 21 moves him to the court of the guard with a standing ration of one round loaf a day from the street of the bakers, for as long as bread lasted in the city. Ancient cities grouped a trade into one street. The clause about bread running out is the siege famine arriving in a single line.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to pray for deliverance, but Jeremiah warns that Pharaoh's army will return to Egypt and the Babylonians will capture Jerusalem; after Jeremiah is arrested trying to leave the city, Zedekiah moves him from a dungeon to the courtyard of the guard.

stories.title: 🕳️ Jeremiah 38
summaryBullets: Now Shephatiah son of Mattan, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur son of Malchijah heard that Jeremiah had been telling all the people: (38:1).

“This is what the LORD says: Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague, but whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live; he will retain his life like a spoil of war, and he will live. (38:2).
This is what the LORD says: This city will surely be delivered into the hands of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it.” (38:3).

Then the officials said to the king, “This man ought to die, for he is discouraging the warriors who remain in this city, as well as all the people, by speaking such words to them; this man is not seeking the well-being of these people, but their ruin.” (38:4).
“Here he is,” replied King Zedekiah. “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.” (38:5).

So they took Jeremiah and dropped him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king’s son, which was in the courtyard of the guard. They lowered Jeremiah with ropes into the cistern, which had no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud. (38:6).
Now Ebed-melech the Cushite, a court official in the royal palace, heard that Jeremiah had been put into the cistern. While the king was sitting at the Gate of Benjamin, (38:7).
Ebed-melech went out from the king’s palace and said to the king, (38:8).

“My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They have dropped him into the cistern, where he will starve to death, for there is no more bread in the city.” (38:9).
So the king commanded Ebed-melech the Cushite, “Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.” (38:10).

Then Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the king’s palace, to a place below the storehouse. From there he took old rags and worn-out clothes and lowered them with ropes to Jeremiah in the cistern. (38:11).
Ebed-melech the Cushite cried out to Jeremiah, “Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes.” Jeremiah did so, (38:12).
and they pulled him up with the ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard. (38:13).

Then King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance to the house of the LORD. “I am going to ask you something,” said the king to Jeremiah. “Do not hide anything from me.” (38:14).
“If I tell you,” Jeremiah replied, “you will surely put me to death. And even if I give you advice, you will not listen to me.” (38:15).

But King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (38:16).

Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “This is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you indeed surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive. (38:17).

But if you do not surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then this city will be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans. They will burn it down, and you yourself will not escape their grasp.’” (38:18).
But King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.” (38:19).
“They will not hand you over,” Jeremiah replied. “Obey the voice of the LORD in what I am telling you, that it may go well with you and you may live. (38:20).
But if you refuse to surrender, this is the word that the LORD has shown me: (38:21).

All the women who remain in the palace of the king of Judah will be brought out to the officials of the king of Babylon, and those women will say: ‘They misled you and overcame you — those trusted friends of yours. Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.’ (38:22).

All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans. And you yourself will not escape their grasp, for you will be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city will be burned down.” (38:23).
Then Zedekiah warned Jeremiah, “Do not let anyone know about this conversation, or you will die. (38:24).
If the officials hear that I have spoken with you, and they come and demand of you, ‘Tell us what you said to the king and what he said to you; do not hide it from us, or we will kill you,’ (38:25).
then tell them, ‘I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.’” (38:26).

When all the officials came to Jeremiah and questioned him, he relayed to them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. So they said no more to him, for no one had overheard the conversation. (38:27).
And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured. (38:28).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 37:15-21: The earlier imprisonment and the daily bread ration, the arrangement the officials overturn here.
Genesis 37:23-24: Joseph stripped and thrown into a pit that had no water in it.
Jeremiah 39:15-18: The promise to Ebed-melech that he will not fall by the sword, because he trusted the LORD.
Psalm 69:1-2: Sinking in deep mire where there is no foothold, the same predicament as 38:6.
2 Kings 25:4-7: Zedekiah's flight and capture, exactly what 38:17-23 warned would happen if he refused to surrender.

translationNotes.note: A private water cistern inside the palace compound: a bottle-shaped shaft cut into rock, narrow at the neck and wide below, plastered to hold winter runoff. Verse 6 says they let him down by ropes and there was no water in it, only mud. That is a cistern at the end of the dry season with the sediment left in the bottom. The shape is the trap. You cannot climb walls that curve out above you.

The name means servant of the king and is a title as much as a name. He is a court official from Cush, the kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, and 38:7 has him go straight out to the king sitting in the Benjamin Gate and say the officials have acted wickedly. The one man in the chapter who acts to save the prophet is a foreigner in the palace, and 39:16-18 is God's word to him by name.

translationNotes.term: Rags and worn-out clothes under the armpits
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 is a detail no summary keeps. Ebed-melech collects castoff cloth from a storeroom under the treasury, sends it down on the ropes, and tells Jeremiah to pad his armpits before they pull. Ropes under the arms take the whole weight of a man on two thin lines; without padding they cut. Jeremiah had been in the mud for some time and could not have taken the lift otherwise.

translationNotes.term: Thirty men to pull him out
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 has the king assign thirty men to the rescue. That is not the manpower needed to lift one starving prisoner; it is an escort. The officials who put him there were powerful enough that the king says openly in 38:5 that he cannot oppose them, so the party has to be large enough that nobody interferes.

translationNotes.term: A secret interview at the third entrance
translationNotes.note: Verses 14-27 show the state of Zedekiah's authority. The king summons the prophet to a side entrance of the temple, swears a private oath not to hand him over, admits he is afraid of the Judeans who have already deserted, and then coaches Jeremiah on what to tell the officials if they ask. The cover story in 38:26 was true as far as it went, and 37:20 is the request it refers to.

stories.keyTakeaway: Four officials convince King Zedekiah to throw Jeremiah into a mud cistern for discouraging the people, but Ebed-Melek rescues him. Later Zedekiah secretly consults Jeremiah, who urges surrender to Babylon to save his life and the city, though the king fears the Jews who have already defected.

stories.title: 🕳️ Jeremiah 39
summaryBullets: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army and laid siege to the city. (39:1).
And on the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year, the city was breached. (39:2).

Then all the officials of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer of Samgar, Nebo-sarsekim the Rabsaris, Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the rest of the officials of the king of Babylon. (39:3).

When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled. They left the city at night by way of the king’s garden, through the gate between the two walls, and they went out along the route to the Arabah. (39:4).

But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They seized him and brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where he pronounced judgment on him. (39:5).
There at Riblah the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and he also killed all the nobles of Judah. (39:6).
Then he put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him with bronze chains to take him to Babylon. (39:7).
The Chaldeans set fire to the palace of the king and to the houses of the people, and they broke down the walls of Jerusalem. (39:8).
Then Nebuzaradan captain of the guard carried away to Babylon the remnant of the people who had remained in the city, along with the deserters who had defected to him. (39:9).
But Nebuzaradan left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had no property, and at that time he gave them vineyards and fields. (39:10).
Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had given orders about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, saying, (39:11).
“Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him; do for him whatever he says.” (39:12).
So Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rabsaris, Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the captains of the king of Babylon (39:13).
had Jeremiah brought from the courtyard of the guard, and they turned him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to take him home. So Jeremiah remained among his own people. (39:14).
And while Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard, the word of the LORD had come to him: (39:15).

“Go and tell Ebed-melech the Cushite that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good, and on that day they will be fulfilled before your eyes. (39:16).
But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear. (39:17).
For I will surely rescue you so that you do not fall by the sword. Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD.’” (39:18).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:1-12: The parallel account of the breach, the burning of the temple and palace, and the deportation.
2 Chronicles 36:17-21: The same fall told with the temple treasures carried off and the land keeping its sabbaths.
Jeremiah 52:4-16: Jeremiah's own closing account of the siege, with the dates and the officers named.
Ezekiel 12:12-13: The prince carried to Babylon in a net, yet not seeing the land with his eyes, matching the blinding at Riblah.
2 Kings 23:33: Riblah in the land of Hamath, where Pharaoh Neco had earlier put Jehoahaz in chains.

translationNotes.note: Verses 1-2 give both ends of it by regnal year: the army arrives in the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, and the wall is breached on the ninth day of the fourth month of his eleventh. That is roughly two years of encirclement, broken once when the Egyptian army came up and the Babylonians pulled back, as 37:5-11 records. The city fell in 586 BC. 52:6 adds that by the fourth month the famine was so severe there was no food at all for the people of the land.

translationNotes.term: Riblah in the land of Hamath
translationNotes.note: A town on the Orontes river in what is now Syria, roughly two hundred miles (320 km) north of Jerusalem, on the main road between Mesopotamia and Egypt with good water and forage. Both Egypt and Babylon used it as a forward army headquarters. Pharaoh Neco put Jehoahaz in chains there in 2 Kings 23:33, and Nebuchadnezzar ran this campaign from it. It is why Zedekiah, captured near Jericho, had to be marched north before he was sentenced.

translationNotes.term: Blinded and bound in bronze fetters
translationNotes.note: Verses 6-7 record the sentence in the order it was carried out: his sons killed in front of him, the nobles of Judah killed, and then his eyes put out. The blinding comes last so that the killing of his sons is the last thing he ever sees. Assyrian and Babylonian records and palace reliefs show the blinding of captive rulers as standard practice for a vassal who broke his oath.

translationNotes.term: The poorest of the people were left
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 says Nebuzaradan left those who owned nothing and gave them vineyards and fields on the spot. Empires deported the useful classes, the officials, soldiers, priests and craftsmen, and left the landless behind to keep the ground in production and the tax revenue flowing. 2 Kings 24:14 records the same policy in 597 BC.

Verse 14 has Jeremiah taken out of the guard court and handed to Gedaliah. Nebuchadnezzar's own order in 39:11-12 was to look after him and do him no harm, which reads oddly until you remember that Jeremiah had spent the siege telling Jerusalem to surrender. To the Babylonians he looked like an asset. 40:2-5 has the Babylonian commander offering him a place in Babylon, which he refuses.

stories.keyTakeaway: Babylon breaches Jerusalem's walls; Zedekiah flees but is captured, his sons are killed before him, and his eyes are put out before he is taken to Babylon. The city is burned and its people exiled, though Nebuchadnezzar orders Jeremiah's protection and release to Gedaliah, and the Lord promises to rescue Ebed-Melek the Cushite.

stories.title: 🏞️ Jeremiah 40
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan captain of the guard had released him at Ramah, having found him bound in chains among all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon. (40:1).
The captain of the guard found Jeremiah and said to him, “The LORD your God decreed this disaster on this place, (40:2).
and now the LORD has fulfilled it; He has done just as He said. Because you people have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed His voice, this thing has happened to you. (40:3).

But now, behold, I am freeing you today from the chains that were on your wrists. If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you. But if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, go no farther. Look, the whole land is before you. Wherever it seems good and right to you, go there.” (40:4).

But before Jeremiah turned to go, Nebuzaradan added, “Return to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon has appointed over the cities of Judah, and stay with him among the people, or go anywhere else that seems right.” Then the captain of the guard gave him a ration and a gift and released him. (40:5).
So Jeremiah went to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah and stayed with him among the people who were left in the land. (40:6).

When all the commanders and men of the armies in the field heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over the land and that he had put him in charge of the men, women, and children who were the poorest of the land and had not been exiled to Babylon, (40:7).

they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah — Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah son of the Maacathite — they and their men. (40:8).

Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, swore an oath to them and their men, assuring them, “Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you. (40:9).

As for me, I will stay in Mizpah to represent you before the Chaldeans who come to us. As for you, gather wine grapes, summer fruit, and oil, place them in your storage jars, and live in the cities you have taken.” (40:10).

When all the Jews in Moab, Ammon, Edom, and all the other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, over them, (40:11).
they all returned from all the places to which they had been banished and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered an abundance of wine grapes and summer fruit. (40:12).
Meanwhile, Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the armies in the field came to Gedaliah at Mizpah (40:13).
and said to him, “Are you aware that Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?” But Gedaliah son of Ahikam did not believe them. (40:14).

Then Johanan son of Kareah spoke privately to Gedaliah at Mizpah. “Let me go and kill Ishmael son of Nethaniah,” he said. “No one will know it. Why should he take your life and scatter all the people of Judah who have gathered to you, so that the remnant of Judah would perish?” (40:15).
But Gedaliah son of Ahikam said to Johanan son of Kareah, “Do not do such a thing! What you are saying about Ishmael is a lie.” (40:16).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:22-24: The parallel account of Gedaliah's appointment and his pledge to the captains and their men.
Jeremiah 26:24: Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from the crowd; Gedaliah is Ahikam's son.
1 Samuel 7:5-6: Samuel gathers all Israel to Mizpah to draw water, fast and confess, the town's earlier standing.
1 Kings 15:22: Asa fortifies Mizpah with the stone and timber of Ramah, which is how it became a stronghold.
Jeremiah 39:11-14: Nebuchadnezzar's order that Jeremiah be looked after, the reason for the release here.

translationNotes.note: The name means watchtower, and the town sat on a height in Benjamin about eight miles (13 km) north of Jerusalem, commanding the road up from the capital. Samuel judged Israel there and Saul was made king there, in 1 Samuel 7:5-6 and 10:17-24, and Asa turned it into a border fortress in 1 Kings 15:22. With Jerusalem burned, the Babylonians made it the seat of the province, which is why the survivors gather there in 40:6-12.

A town about five miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem on the main road, used here as the muster camp where prisoners were chained and sorted before the march to Babylon. Verse 1 has Jeremiah found in that column, in irons, and pulled out of it. Ramah is the same place 31:15 names for the voice of Rachel weeping.

Gedaliah is a native Judean appointed by Babylon to administer the province, not a king. Empires routinely governed a conquered territory through a local man of standing. A clay seal impression reading belonging to Gedalyahu, who is over the house is known from the ruins of Lachish; that title marks the chief officer of a royal household.

translationNotes.term: Gather wine grapes, summer fruit and oil
translationNotes.note: Verse 10 is an instruction to bring in a harvest, and 40:12 records that they did, in abundance. The war had run through two growing seasons with nobody tending the vineyards, and the remnant walked back into an unpicked crop. It is the one moment of ordinary life in the last chapters of the book, and chapter 41 ends it.

Verse 14 names the Ammonite king as the man who sent Ishmael to kill Gedaliah. Ammon lay east of the Jordan and had joined the anti-Babylon coalition of 27:3; a Babylonian province next door under a compliant governor was against its interest. A seal impression carrying the name Baalyisha, servant of the king, has been recovered in Jordan.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah from chains and directs him to Gedaliah at Mizpah, where Gedaliah is appointed governor over the remaining people; when scattered Jews return and the land becomes productive, Johanan warns Gedaliah that Ishmael son of Nethaniah plots against him, but Gedaliah refuses to believe it.

stories.title: 🏞️ Jeremiah 41
summaryBullets: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, who was a member of the royal family and one of the king’s chief officers, came with ten men to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah, and they ate a meal together there. (41:1).

Then Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the ten men who were with him got up and struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, with the sword, killing the one whom the king of Babylon had appointed to govern the land. (41:2).
Ishmael also killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, as well as the Chaldean soldiers who were there. (41:3).
On the second day after the murder of Gedaliah, when no one yet knew about it, (41:4).

eighty men who had shaved off their beards, torn their garments, and cut themselves came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, carrying grain offerings and frankincense for the house of the LORD. (41:5).
And Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he went. When Ishmael encountered the men, he said, “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” (41:6).
And when they came into the city, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and threw them into a cistern. (41:7).
But ten of the men among them said to Ishmael, “Do not kill us, for we have hidden treasure in the field— wheat, barley, oil, and honey!” So he refrained from killing them with the others. (41:8).

Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men he had struck down along with Gedaliah was a large one that King Asa had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain. (41:9).

Then Ishmael took captive all the remnant of the people of Mizpah— the daughters of the king along with all the others who remained in Mizpah— over whom Nebuzaradan captain of the guard had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Ishmael son of Nethaniah took them captive and set off to cross over to the Ammonites. (41:10).
When Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the armies with him heard of all the crimes that Ishmael son of Nethaniah had committed, (41:11).
they took all their men and went to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah. And they found him near the great pool in Gibeon. (41:12).
When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the army with him, they rejoiced, (41:13).
and all the people whom Ishmael had taken captive at Mizpah turned and went over to Johanan son of Kareah. (41:14).
But Ishmael son of Nethaniah and eight of his men escaped from Johanan and went to the Ammonites. (41:15).

Then Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the armies with him took the whole remnant of the people from Mizpah whom he had recovered from Ishmael son of Nethaniah after Ishmael had killed Gedaliah son of Ahikam: the soldiers, women, children, and court officials he had brought back from Gibeon. (41:16).
And they went and stayed in Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, in order to proceed into Egypt (41:17).
to escape the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of the Chaldeans because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land. (41:18).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:25-26: The parallel account of the murder at Mizpah and the flight of the whole people to Egypt.
1 Kings 15:16-22: Asa builds up Mizpah against Baasha of Israel, the fortification works that cut the cistern of 41:9.
Jeremiah 40:13-16: Johanan's warning that Ishmael was sent by Baalis, which Gedaliah refused to believe.
Zechariah 7:5: A fast kept in the seventh month all through the exile, the month in which Gedaliah was killed.
1 Samuel 10:17-24: Saul presented as king at Mizpah, an earlier national assembly on the same hill.

translationNotes.term: They ate a meal together there
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 puts the killing at a shared table. Eating with a man in the ancient Near East placed him under your protection for as long as he was your guest; Psalm 41:9 counts betrayal at a meal as the sharpest kind. Ishmael kills the governor who had just fed him, and 41:2 says it was done with the sword by men who had eaten the same bread.

translationNotes.term: Eighty men with beards shaved and clothes torn
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 describes pilgrims coming down from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria with grain offerings and incense, in full mourning dress: beards shaved off, garments ripped, bodies gashed. They are northerners still bringing offerings to a temple that had been burned months earlier, walking toward a sanctuary that no longer stood.

translationNotes.term: The cistern King Asa had made
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 identifies the pit by its builder. Asa fortified Mizpah against Baasha of Israel in the early ninth century BC, and a fortress needs stored water, so the cistern was cut as part of those works. Ishmael filled a two-hundred-year-old rock-cut water tank with bodies, which poisoned the town's water supply along with everything else.

Verse 12 names the place where Johanan caught up with Ishmael. Gibeon lies a couple of miles from Mizpah, and the pool there is the one 2 Samuel 2:13 puts Abner and Joab's men beside. A great rock-cut shaft with a spiral stair descending to water has been excavated at the site, more than eighty feet (25 m) deep.

Verse 17 names the staging camp on the road south. Chimham was the son of Barzillai the Gileadite, whom David took to Jerusalem with him in 2 Samuel 19:37-40; the name attached to a piece of ground near Bethlehem and stuck for four centuries. It is a lodging place on the caravan route to Egypt, which is where they are heading.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ishmael son of Nethaniah assassinates Gedaliah the governor and massacres the men with him at Mizpah, then takes captives including the king's daughters; Johanan son of Kareah pursues and defeats him, recovers the captives, and leads the survivors toward Egypt to escape Babylonian retaliation.

stories.title: 🗺️ Jeremiah 42
summaryBullets: Then all the commanders of the forces, along with Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, approached (42:1).

Jeremiah the prophet and said, “May our petition come before you; pray to the LORD your God on behalf of this entire remnant. For few of us remain of the many, as you can see with your own eyes. (42:2).
Pray that the LORD your God will tell us the way we should walk and the thing we should do.” (42:3).

“I have heard you,” replied Jeremiah the prophet. “I will surely pray to the LORD your God as you request, and I will tell you everything that the LORD answers. I will not withhold a word from you.” (42:4).
Then they said to Jeremiah, “May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act upon every word that the LORD your God sends you to tell us. (42:5).
Whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, so that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God!” (42:6).
After ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, (42:7).
and he summoned Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest. (42:8).
Jeremiah told them, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your petition: (42:9).
‘If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you, for I will relent of the disaster I have brought upon you. (42:10).
Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear; do not be afraid of him, declares the LORD, for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him. (42:11).
And I will show you compassion, and he will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land.’ (42:12).
But if you say, ‘We will not stay in this land,’ and you thus disobey the voice of the LORD your God, (42:13).
and if you say, ‘No, but we will go to the land of Egypt and live there, where we will not see war or hear the sound of the ram’s horn or hunger for bread,’ (42:14).
then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah! This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you are determined to go to Egypt and reside there, (42:15).
then the sword you fear will overtake you there, and the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt, and you will die there. (42:16).
So all who resolve to go to Egypt to reside there will die by sword and famine and plague. Not one of them will survive or escape the disaster I will bring upon them.’ (42:17).

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Just as My anger and wrath were poured out on the residents of Jerusalem, so will My wrath be poured out on you if you go to Egypt. You will become an object of cursing and horror, of vilification and disgrace, and you will never see this place again.’ (42:18).
The LORD has told you, O remnant of Judah, ‘Do not go to Egypt.’ Know for sure that I have warned you today! (42:19).

For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God, saying, ‘Pray to the LORD our God on our behalf, and as for all that the LORD our God says, tell it to us and we will do it.’ (42:20).
For I have told you today, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in all He has sent me to tell you. (42:21).
Now therefore, know for sure that by sword and famine and plague you will die in the place where you desire to go to reside.” (42:22).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 17:16: A king must not send the people back to Egypt for horses, since the LORD said you shall never return that way.
Isaiah 31:1: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and lean on horses rather than on the Holy One of Israel.
Numbers 14:1-4: Israel in the wilderness proposes to choose a leader and go back to Egypt.
Jeremiah 1:10: To build and to plant, the restoration pair God offers the remnant in 42:10.
Jeremiah 40:9-10: Gedaliah's earlier promise that staying in the land and serving Babylon would go well with them.

translationNotes.note: Verse 7 records a ten-day gap between the question and the answer. Jeremiah did not produce an oracle on demand, and the book keeps the interval in the record. The delay matters to the story: 42:5-6 has the people swearing in advance to obey whatever comes, and they had ten days to think about that oath before they broke it.

The same verb as the potter's house in 18:8. Verse 10 says God has relented of the disaster He inflicted, and offers to build and plant them where they stand. The offer is conditional on one thing only, staying in the land under Babylonian rule, and 42:13-18 gives the alternative in the same detail.

translationNotes.term: Sword, famine and plague in Egypt
translationNotes.note: Verses 16-17 take the three things the remnant is fleeing and place them at the destination. The argument is that the danger is not geographic. The same trio runs through the book at 14:12, 21:9, 24:10 and 44:13, and 44:27-28 reports the outcome: only a few fugitives came back.

translationNotes.term: You have gone astray at the cost of your lives
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 charges them with using the inquiry as cover. They had asked for a word and sworn to obey it, and 43:2 shows the decision was already made, since the answer is met not with argument but with the claim that Jeremiah is lying. The Hebrew in 42:20 says they went astray in their own souls, meaning they deceived themselves before anyone else.

stories.keyTakeaway: Johanan and the army officers ask Jeremiah to seek God's guidance on whether they should stay in Judah or flee; after ten days, Jeremiah delivers God's word promising protection if they remain but warning of death by sword and famine if they go to Egypt, then declares that their disobedience to this message will prove fatal.

headings.text: A Warning against Going to Egypt

stories.title: 🗺️ Jeremiah 43
summaryBullets: When Jeremiah had finished telling all the people all the words of the LORD their God— everything that the LORD had sent him to say— (43:1).

Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the arrogant men said to Jeremiah, “You are lying! The LORD our God has not sent you to say, ‘You must not go to Egypt to reside there.’ (43:2).
Rather, Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us to deliver us into the hands of the Chaldeans, so that they may put us to death or exile us to Babylon!” (43:3).
So Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces disobeyed the command of the LORD to stay in the land of Judah. (43:4).

Instead, Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took the whole remnant of Judah, those who had returned to the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been scattered, (43:5).

the men, the women, the children, the king’s daughters, and everyone whom Nebuzaradan captain of the guard had allowed to remain with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, as well as Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah. (43:6).
So they entered the land of Egypt because they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and they went as far as Tahpanhes. (43:7).
Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah at Tahpanhes: (43:8).
“In the sight of the Jews, pick up some large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace at Tahpanhes. (43:9).

Then tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and I will set his throne over these stones that I have embedded, and he will spread his royal pavilion over them. (43:10).
He will come and strike down the land of Egypt, bringing death to those destined for death, captivity to those destined for captivity, and the sword to those destined for the sword. (43:11).

I will kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take their gods as captives. So he will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and he will depart from there unscathed. (43:12).
He will demolish the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun in the land of Egypt, and he will burn down the temples of the gods of Egypt.’” (43:13).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 42:13-18: The exact warning they are now rejecting, that the sword they fear will overtake them in Egypt.
Jeremiah 46:13-19: The oracle that Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt, with Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes named.
Ezekiel 29:17-20: Egypt handed to Nebuchadnezzar as the wages for his army after the long labour at Tyre.
Ezekiel 30:13-18: Memphis, Pathros, Zoan and Tahpanhes each named in the judgment on Egypt.
Isaiah 19:1-4: The LORD rides on a swift cloud into Egypt and the idols of Egypt tremble before Him.

translationNotes.note: A frontier fortress in the eastern Nile delta, called Daphnae by the Greeks, on the military road that runs from Canaan into Egypt. It was the first Egyptian strongpoint a party coming down from Judah would reach, with a garrison and a royal residence. Refugees stopped there because it was the border, which is why the Judean community forms at that spot in 43:7.

translationNotes.term: The brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace
translationNotes.note: A paved forecourt of mud brick outside the building. Verse 9 has Jeremiah press large stones into the clay of it in front of witnesses, and 43:10 says Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on those stones and spread his canopy over them. An eastern king held court under an awning in an open courtyard, so the sign marks the exact patch of ground where the conqueror's tent will stand.

Verse 3 accuses Baruch of inciting Jeremiah to hand them over to the Chaldeans. It is the only place where the scribe is charged as the real author of the message, and it shows how visible Baruch had become since chapter 36. Both men are then taken to Egypt against their will, according to 43:6.

Verse 13 says he will smash the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun in Egypt. The Hebrew names it House of the Sun, the city the Greeks called Heliopolis, north of modern Cairo, the ancient centre of the sun-god's worship. Its standing stone obelisks were the marker of the cult, and breaking them is naming the target precisely.

stories.keyTakeaway: Johanan and the other leaders reject Jeremiah's warning against going to Egypt, accuse him of lying, and force him and Baruch to travel with them to Tahpanhes. There, God tells Jeremiah to bury stones at Pharaoh's palace and prophesy that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt and destroy its temples.

stories.title: 🏺 Jeremiah 44
summaryBullets: This is the word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews living in the land of Egypt— in Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Memphis— and in the land of Pathros: (44:1).

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: You have seen all the disaster that I brought against Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah; and behold, they lie today in ruins and desolation (44:2).
because of the evil they have done. They provoked Me to anger by continuing to burn incense and to serve other gods that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew. (44:3).
Yet I sent you all My servants the prophets again and again, saying: ‘Do not do this detestable thing that I hate.’ (44:4).
But they did not listen or incline their ears; they did not turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods. (44:5).
Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, so that they have become the desolate ruin they are today. (44:6).

So now, this is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves by cutting off from Judah man and woman, child and infant, leaving yourselves without a remnant? (44:7).

Why are you provoking Me to anger by the work of your hands by burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt, where you have gone to reside? As a result, you will be cut off and will become an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth. (44:8).

Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers and of the kings of Judah and their wives, as well as the wickedness that you and your wives committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? (44:9).
To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence, nor have they followed My instruction or the statutes that I set before you and your fathers. (44:10).
Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I will set My face to bring disaster and to cut off all Judah. (44:11).

And I will take away the remnant of Judah who have resolved to go to the land of Egypt to reside there; they will meet their end. They will all fall by the sword or be consumed by famine. From the least to the greatest, they will die by sword or famine; and they will become an object of cursing and horror, of vilification and reproach. (44:12).
I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem, by sword and famine and plague, (44:13).

so that none of the remnant of Judah who have gone to reside in Egypt will escape or survive to return to the land of Judah, where they long to return and live; for none will return except a few fugitives.” (44:14).

Then all the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, and all the women standing by— a great assembly— along with all the people living in the land of Egypt and in Pathros, said to Jeremiah, (44:15).
“As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you! (44:16).

Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do: We will burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and offer drink offerings to her, just as we, our fathers, our kings, and our officials did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster. (44:17).
But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine.” (44:18).

“Moreover,” said the women, “when we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands’ knowledge that we made sacrificial cakes in her image and poured out drink offerings to her?” (44:19).
Then Jeremiah said to all the people, both men and women, who were answering him, (44:20).

“As for the incense you burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem— you, your fathers, your kings, your officials, and the people of the land— did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind? (44:21).

So the LORD could no longer endure the evil deeds and detestable acts you committed, and your land became a desolation, a horror, and an object of cursing, without inhabitant, as it is this day. (44:22).

Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in His instruction, His statutes, and His testimonies, this disaster has befallen you, as you see today.” (44:23).
Then Jeremiah said to all the people, including all the women, “Hear the word of the LORD, all those of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. (44:24).

This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: As for you and your wives, you have spoken with your mouths and fulfilled with your hands your words: ‘We will surely perform our vows that we have made to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.’ Go ahead, then, do what you have promised! Keep your vows! (44:25).

Nevertheless, hear the word of the LORD, all you people of Judah living in Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by My great name, says the LORD, that never again will any man of Judah living in the land of Egypt invoke My name or say, ‘As surely as the Lord GOD lives.’ (44:26).
I am watching over them for harm and not for good, and every man of Judah who is in the land of Egypt will meet his end by sword or famine, until they are finished off. (44:27).

Those who escape the sword will return from Egypt to Judah, few in number, and the whole remnant of Judah who went to dwell in the land of Egypt will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs! (44:28).
This will be a sign to you that I will punish you in this place, declares the LORD, so that you may know that My threats of harm against you will surely stand. (44:29).

This is what the LORD says: Behold, I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of his enemies who seek his life, just as I delivered Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the enemy who was seeking his life.” (44:30).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 7:16-20: The earlier rebuke over the queen of heaven, with the whole household described at work.
Exodus 20:3-5: The command against other gods, the statute the vows in 44:17 and 44:25 are made against.
Deuteronomy 4:26-28: A warning that in exile they will serve gods of wood and stone made by human hands.
Ezekiel 29:1-6: Judgment announced against Pharaoh of Egypt, the king whose fall becomes the sign here.
Jeremiah 42:15-18: The warning that going to Egypt would end in sword and famine, now spoken to the people who went.

translationNotes.term: The Queen of Heaven and her cakes
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְלֶכֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם (meleketh ha-shamayim) - Hebrew: כַּוָּנִים (kawwanim)
translationNotes.note: A goddess worshipped with incense, poured drink offerings and baked cakes. Queen of heaven is the standing title of Ishtar in Mesopotamian texts. Verse 19 gives the detail: the women made sacrificial cakes in her image, which means dough pressed in a mould shaped like the goddess, and they say plainly that their husbands knew. 7:18 has the same rite in Jerusalem with the whole family assigned a task.

translationNotes.term: We had plenty of food and saw no disaster
translationNotes.note: Verses 17-18 are the clearest statement of the people's own reasoning anywhere in the book. Their argument is economic: while they burned incense to her they ate well, and since they stopped they have lost everything. They date the turn to Josiah's reforms and read the disasters that followed as the goddess's answer. Verses 20-23 give the counter-argument in the same terms.

Verse 1 maps the Judean settlements across Egypt. Migdol and Tahpanhes are frontier posts in the eastern delta, Memphis is the old capital at the head of the delta near modern Cairo, and Pathros is Upper Egypt, the long southern stretch of the Nile valley. From border fort to the far south, the exiles had spread the whole length of the country.

The Egyptian king called Apries in Greek sources, who ruled from about 589 to 570 BC. He sent the relief army that briefly lifted the siege of Jerusalem in 37:5. Verse 30 makes his fall the confirming sign of this oracle. He was overthrown after a mutiny in his army and died in the hands of his own countrymen, and his successor Amasis took the throne.

Verses 27-28 narrow the survivors twice. Of those who went down to Egypt, a small number of fugitives will return to Judah, and 44:28 says they will know whose word stands, His or theirs. The book ends its account of the Egyptian community with a handful walking back the way they came.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judeans in Egypt openly refuse to stop worshiping the ‘queen of heaven.’ Jeremiah declares judgment and gives a sign: Hophra’s fall will confirm it.

headings.text: Judgment on the Jews in Egypt

stories.title: 📜 Jeremiah 45
summaryBullets: This is the word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when he wrote these words on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: (45:1).
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says to you, Baruch: (45:2).
You have said, ‘Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain! I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest.’” (45:3).
Thus Jeremiah was to say to Baruch: “This is what the LORD says: Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted. (45:4).

But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking! For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD, but wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.” (45:5).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 36:1-8: Baruch takes the dictation and reads the scroll in the temple, the writing this word is dated to.
Jeremiah 36:26: The king orders Baruch and Jeremiah seized, and the LORD hides them, the danger behind 45:3.
Jeremiah 1:10: To pluck up and to break down, to build and to plant, the commission 45:4 turns back on the whole earth.
Jeremiah 39:18: Your life will be your prize of war, the same idiom of survival granted to Ebed-melech.
Jeremiah 43:1-7: Baruch accused of steering the prophet, and carried down to Egypt with him.

translationNotes.note: A professional scribe of high family. His brother Seraiah is the quartermaster who carries a scroll to Babylon in 51:59, and both are grandsons of Mahseiah, so Baruch came from the administrative class. He writes the scroll in chapter 36, reads it publicly, keeps the second copy, holds the deed of purchase in 32:12-16, and is deported to Egypt in 43:6. He is the most fully documented scribe in the Old Testament.

The trade meant more than copying. A scribe cut and trimmed his own reed pens, ground and mixed carbon ink, prepared and joined papyrus sheets or skins into a roll, ruled and laid out the columns, took dictation at speed, read a document aloud in public, and drew up and witnessed legal instruments. Every one of those tasks shows up in Baruch's story between chapters 32 and 45.

translationNotes.term: Woe is me, for the LORD has added sorrow
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 is Baruch's own complaint, preserved as spoken: he is worn out with groaning and finds no rest. The word to him is one of the shortest units in the book, five verses long, and it answers a man's private exhaustion rather than a national crisis.

translationNotes.term: Do not seek great things for yourself
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 is not a rule against ambition in general; it is a word to one man at one time, and the reason follows in the same sentence. God is tearing down what He built across the whole earth, so this is not the season for a career. What Baruch gets instead is stated in 45:5: his life, wherever he goes.

Verse 1 dates this word to 605 BC, the same year as the scroll of 36:1 and the Carchemish oracle of 46:2. Chapter 45 sits near the end of the book but belongs some eighteen years before the fall of Jerusalem. The scroll was placed here, at the close of Jeremiah's own words, rather than in its chronological slot.

stories.keyTakeaway: Baruch is warned not to chase status amid national judgment. God promises him survival; his life as the spoil he carries out.

stories.title: 🛡️ Jeremiah 46
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD about the nations— the word that came to Jeremiah the prophet (46:1).

concerning Egypt and the army of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, which was defeated at Carchemish on the Euphrates River by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah: (46:2).
“Deploy your shields, small and large; advance for battle! (46:3).
Harness the horses; mount the steeds; take your positions with helmets on! Polish your spears; put on armor! (46:4).
Why am I seeing this? They are terrified, they are retreating; their warriors are defeated, they flee in haste without looking back; terror is on every side!” declares the LORD. (46:5).
“The swift cannot flee, and the warrior cannot escape! In the north by the River Euphrates they stumble and fall. (46:6).
Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters churn? (46:7).
Egypt rises like the Nile, and its waters churn like rivers, boasting, ‘I will rise and cover the earth; I will destroy the cities and their people.’ (46:8).
Advance, O horses! Race furiously, O chariots! Let the warriors come forth— Cush and Put carrying their shields, men of Lydia drawing the bow. (46:9).

For that day belongs to the Lord GOD of Hosts, a day of vengeance against His foes. The sword will devour until it is satisfied, until it is quenched with their blood. For the Lord GOD of Hosts will hold a sacrifice in the land of the north by the River Euphrates. (46:10).
Go up to Gilead for balm, O Virgin Daughter of Egypt! In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing. (46:11).
The nations have heard of your shame, and your outcry fills the earth, because warrior stumbles over warrior and both of them have fallen together.” (46:12).
This is the word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: (46:13).
“Announce it in Egypt, and proclaim it in Migdol; proclaim it in Memphis and Tahpanhes: ‘Take your positions and prepare yourself, for the sword devours those around you.’ (46:14).
Why have your warriors been laid low? They cannot stand, for the LORD has thrust them down. (46:15).
They continue to stumble; indeed, they have fallen over one another. They say, ‘Get up! Let us return to our people and to the land of our birth, away from the sword of the oppressor.’ (46:16).
There they will cry out: ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt was all noise; he has let the appointed time pass him by.’ (46:17).
As surely as I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts, there will come one who is like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea. (46:18).
Pack your bags for exile, O daughter dwelling in Egypt! For Memphis will be laid waste, destroyed and uninhabited. (46:19).
Egypt is a beautiful heifer, but a gadfly from the north is coming against her. (46:20).

Even the mercenaries among her are like fattened calves. They too will turn back; together they will flee, they will not stand their ground, for the day of calamity is coming upon them — the time of their punishment. (46:21).
Egypt will hiss like a fleeing serpent, for the enemy will advance in force; with axes they will come against her like woodsmen cutting down trees. (46:22).
They will chop down her forest, declares the LORD, dense though it may be, for they are more numerous than locusts; they cannot be counted. (46:23).
The Daughter of Egypt will be put to shame; she will be delivered into the hands of the people of the north.” (46:24).
The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I am about to punish Amon god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh, Egypt with her gods and kings, and those who trust in Pharaoh. (46:25).

I will deliver them into the hands of those who seek their lives— of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. But after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old, declares the LORD. (46:26).

But you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed, O Israel. For I will surely save you out of a distant place, your descendants from the land of their captivity! Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid. (46:27).

And you, My servant Jacob, do not be afraid, declares the LORD, for I am with you. Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have banished you, I will not completely destroy you. Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” (46:28).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 23:29-30: Pharaoh Neco marches to the Euphrates and kills Josiah at Megiddo on the way.
2 Chronicles 35:20-24: The same battle told at length, with Josiah refusing Neco's warning and dying of his wounds.
2 Kings 24:7: The king of Egypt does not march out again, because Babylon had taken all his territory to the Euphrates.
Nahum 3:8-10: Thebes on the Nile sacked and its people carried into exile, held up as a warning to Nineveh.
Jeremiah 30:10-11: Almost word for word the same promise that Jacob will return and be quiet, and God will not make a full end.

translationNotes.note: A fortified city commanding the main ford of the Euphrates in northern Syria, on what is now the Turkish border. Whoever held it controlled the road between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the Egyptian army there, ending Egypt's claim on Syria and Canaan in a single day. Verse 2 dates the oracle to that battle, and 2 Kings 24:7 states the result.

Neco II, king of Egypt from about 610 to 595 BC. He was marching north to prop up the last of Assyria when Josiah intercepted him at Megiddo and was killed, according to 2 Kings 23:29 and 2 Chronicles 35:20-24. Neco then deposed Josiah's son Jehoahaz and put Jehoiakim on the throne of Judah, so the army wrecked at Carchemish belonged to the king who had been appointing Judah's kings.

translationNotes.term: Buckler and shield, coats of mail and lances
translationNotes.note: Verses 3-4 are a muster order shouted through a camp: bring up the small shield and the large one, harness the horses, mount, fall in with helmets on, polish the spears, put on the armour. The small buckler was strapped to the arm; the large shield covered a man standing. Verse 9 then names the contingents, Cush and Put with shields and the Ludim drawing the bow, which is a mercenary army.

Verses 7-8 use the one event that defined Egyptian life. The Nile rose every summer, spilled over its banks and laid down the silt that made the country farmable. To say Egypt is rising like the river and means to cover the earth is to use Egypt's own image of itself, and verse 8 puts the boast in Egypt's mouth before it collapses.

Thebes, called No in Hebrew, lay on the Nile some four hundred miles (640 km) south of the delta and held the vast temple complex of Amon, chief god of the Egyptian state. Nahum 3:8-10 describes its sack by Assyria in 663 BC as a thing everybody knew about. Verse 25 names the god, the city, Pharaoh and those who trust in him in one sentence.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD declares that Pharaoh Necho's army will be defeated at Carchemish and that Nebuchadnezzar will bring destruction to Egypt, its gods, and those who trust in Pharaoh; yet Jacob and Israel are assured they will be saved and restored, though disciplined.

stories.title: 🛡️ Jeremiah 47
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet about the Philistines before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. (47:1).

This is what the LORD says: “See how the waters are rising from the north and becoming an overflowing torrent. They will overflow the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants. The people will cry out, and all who dwell in the land will wail (47:2).
at the sound of the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels. The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp. (47:3).

For the day has come to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every remaining ally. Indeed, the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines, the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor. (47:4).
The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning; Ashkelon will be silenced. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourself? (47:5).
‘Alas, O sword of the LORD, how long until you rest? Return to your sheath; cease and be still!’ (47:6).
How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it? He has appointed it against Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland.” (47:7).
crossRefs: Amos 1:6-8: Oracle against Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron for carrying off a whole population into exile.
Zephaniah 2:4-7: Gaza abandoned and Ashkelon left desolate, the seacoast falling to the remnant of Judah.
Isaiah 14:29-31: A word against Philistia telling the whole land to melt, because smoke comes out of the north.
Amos 9:7: The LORD says He brought the Philistines up from Caphtor, the origin 47:4 names.
Ezekiel 25:15-17: Judgment on the Philistines and the Cherethites for taking revenge with an ancient hatred.

translationNotes.note: A people settled on the coastal plain southwest of Judah in five city-states: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. They arrived by sea and held the plain from the days of the judges; Samson, Samuel, Saul and David all fought them. 1 Samuel 13:19-22 records that they controlled ironworking so tightly that Israelites had to go down to them to have a ploughshare sharpened. Modern English still carries their name in the word Palestine.

The homeland the Philistines came from, named again in Amos 9:7 and Deuteronomy 2:23, and usually understood as Crete and the Aegean islands. Verse 4 calls them the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor, so the oracle is addressing a people the text treats as immigrants from across the sea.

translationNotes.term: Waters rising out of the north
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 pictures the invasion as a flash flood coming down a wadi: a dry channel filling in minutes and carrying off the town and everyone in it. In a country where the winter torrents did exactly that, this is a literal danger used as an image, and the direction, from the north, is the standard line of march for a Mesopotamian army.

Verse 5 reports mourning rites: heads shaved bare, and the coastal people gashing themselves. Shaving the head and cutting the skin were customary signs of grief in the region, and Deuteronomy 14:1 forbids Israel to do either. The verse is describing what the Philistine cities are doing, not prescribing it.

translationNotes.term: Tyre and Sidon cut off from help
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 says the day is coming to destroy every survivor who could help Tyre and Sidon. The Philistine ports and the Phoenician ports were the same commercial network. Cutting off the southern coast strips the northern cities of their allies, which is what chapters 26 to 28 of Ezekiel then describe happening to Tyre.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD announces through Jeremiah that rising waters from the north will devastate the Philistine lands, destroying their towns and people as an instrument of judgment. Gaza and Ashkelon will mourn, and the sword of the LORD will not rest until it has completed its destruction of the Philistines and their coasts.

stories.title: 🍷 Jeremiah 48
summaryBullets: Concerning Moab, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Woe to Nebo, for it will be devastated. Kiriathaim will be captured and disgraced; the fortress will be shattered and dismantled. (48:1).

There is no longer praise for Moab; in Heshbon they devise evil against her: ‘Come, let us cut her off from nationhood.’ You too, O people of Madmen, will be silenced; the sword will pursue you. (48:2).
A voice cries out from Horonaim: ‘Devastation and great destruction!’ (48:3).
Moab will be shattered; her little ones will cry out. (48:4).
For on the ascent to Luhith they weep bitterly as they go, and on the descent to Horonaim cries of distress resound over the destruction: (48:5).
‘Flee! Run for your lives! Become like a juniper in the desert.’ (48:6).
Because you trust in your works and treasures, you too will be captured, and Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials. (48:7).
The destroyer will move against every city, and not one town will escape. The valley will also be ruined, and the high plain will be destroyed, as the LORD has said. (48:8).
Put salt on Moab, for she will be laid waste; her cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them. (48:9).
Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed. (48:10).

Moab has been at ease from youth, settled like wine on its dregs; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel or gone into exile. So his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged. (48:11).
Therefore behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will send to him wanderers, who will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars. (48:12).
Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed when they trusted in Bethel. (48:13).
How can you say, ‘We are warriors, mighty men ready for battle’ ? (48:14).
Moab has been destroyed and its towns have been invaded; the best of its young men have gone down in the slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts. (48:15).
Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly. (48:16).
Mourn for him, all you who surround him, everyone who knows his name; tell how the mighty scepter is shattered — the glorious staff! (48:17).
Come down from your glory; sit on parched ground, O daughter dwelling in Dibon, for the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses. (48:18).
Stand by the road and watch, O dweller of Aroer! Ask the man fleeing or the woman escaping, ‘What has happened?’ (48:19).
Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered. Wail and cry out! Declare by the Arnon that Moab is destroyed. (48:20).
Judgment has come upon the high plain— upon Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath, (48:21).
upon Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, (48:22).
upon Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, (48:23).
upon Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the towns of Moab, those far and near. (48:24).
The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken,” declares the LORD. (48:25).
“Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD; so Moab will wallow in his own vomit, and he will also become a laughingstock. (48:26).
Was not Israel your object of ridicule? Was he ever found among thieves? For whenever you speak of him you shake your head. (48:27).
Abandon the towns and settle among the rocks, O dwellers of Moab! Be like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave. (48:28).
We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart. (48:29).
I know his insolence,” declares the LORD, “but it is futile. His boasting is as empty as his deeds. (48:30).
Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab; I will moan for the men of Kir-heres. (48:31).

I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah, more than I weep for Jazer. Your tendrils have extended to the sea; they reach even to Jazer. The destroyer has descended on your summer fruit and grape harvest. (48:32).

Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard and from the fields of Moab. I have stopped the flow of wine from the presses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; their shouts are not for joy. (48:33).
There is a cry from Heshbon to Elealeh; they raise their voices to Jahaz, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah; for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up. (48:34).
In Moab, declares the LORD, I will bring an end to those who make offerings on the high places and burn incense to their gods. (48:35).
Therefore My heart laments like a flute for Moab; it laments like a flute for the men of Kir-heres, because the wealth they acquired has perished. (48:36).
For every head is shaved and every beard is clipped; on every hand is a gash, and around every waist is sackcloth. (48:37).
On all the rooftops of Moab and in the public squares, everyone is mourning; for I have shattered Moab like an unwanted jar,” declares the LORD. (48:38).
“How shattered it is! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! Moab has become an object of ridicule and horror to all those around him.” (48:39).
For this is what the LORD says: “Behold, an eagle swoops down and spreads his wings against Moab. (48:40).
Kirioth has been taken, and the strongholds seized. In that day the heart of Moab’s warriors will be like the heart of a woman in labor. (48:41).
Moab will be destroyed as a nation because he vaunted himself against the LORD. (48:42).
Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab,” declares the LORD. (48:43).
“Whoever flees the panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare. For I will bring upon Moab the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD. (48:44).

“Those who flee will stand helpless in Heshbon’s shadow, because fire has gone forth from Heshbon and a flame from within Sihon. It devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult. (48:45).
Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished; for your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity. (48:46).
Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,” declares the LORD. Here ends the judgment on Moab. (48:47).
crossRefs: Isaiah 15:1-16:14: The parallel oracle against Moab, town by town, with the same weeping over Nebo and Heshbon.
Genesis 19:36-37: Moab's descent from Lot, which makes Moab and Israel kin.
Numbers 21:27-30: An older poem about the people of Chemosh, whose lines reappear in 48:45-46.
Numbers 22:1-24:25: Balak of Moab hires Balaam to curse Israel on the plains of Moab.
2 Kings 3:26-27: The king of Moab sacrifices his eldest son on the wall when the battle turns against him.
