A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moab’s stability, pride, and wine are overturned; lament rises across its towns, yet a final word of restoration is given.

stories.title: 🏜️ Jeremiah 49
summaryBullets: Concerning the Ammonites, this is what the LORD says: “Has Israel no sons? Is he without heir? Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad? Why have his people settled in their cities? (49:1).

Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sound the battle cry against Rabbah of the Ammonites. It will become a heap of ruins, and its villages will be burned. Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD. (49:2).

Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai has been destroyed; cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth and mourn; run back and forth within your walls, for Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials. (49:3).
Why do you boast of your valleys— your valleys so fruitful, O faithless daughter? You trust in your riches and say, ‘Who can come against me?’ (49:4).
Behold, I am about to bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of Hosts, from all those around you. You will each be driven headlong, with no one to regather the fugitives. (49:5).
Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity,” declares the LORD. (49:6).
Concerning Edom, this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom decayed? (49:7).
Turn and run! Lie low, O dwellers of Dedan, for I will bring disaster on Esau at the time I punish him. (49:8).
If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleanings? Were thieves to come in the night, would they not steal only what they wanted? (49:9).

But I will strip Esau bare; I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself. His descendants will be destroyed along with his relatives and neighbors, and he will be no more. (49:10).
Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me.” (49:11).
For this is what the LORD says: “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too. (49:12).
For by Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that Bozrah will become a desolation, a disgrace, a ruin, and a curse, and all her cities will be in ruins forever.” (49:13).
I have heard a message from the LORD; an envoy has been sent to the nations: “Assemble yourselves to march against her! Rise up for battle!” (49:14).
“For behold, I will make you small among nations, despised among men. (49:15).

The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks, O occupiers of the mountain summit. Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down,” declares the LORD. (49:16).
“Edom will become an object of horror. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds. (49:17).
As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors,” says the LORD, “no one will dwell there; no man will abide there. (49:18).

Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture. For in an instant I will chase Edom from her land. Who is the chosen one I will appoint for this? For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” (49:19).

Therefore hear the plans that the LORD has drawn up against Edom and the strategies He has devised against the people of Teman: Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them. (49:20).
At the sound of their fall the earth will quake; their cry will resound to the Red Sea. (49:21).
Look! An eagle will soar and swoop down, spreading its wings over Bozrah. In that day the hearts of Edom’s mighty men will be like the heart of a woman in labor. (49:22).
Concerning Damascus: “Hamath and Arpad are put to shame, for they have heard a bad report; they are agitated like the sea; their anxiety cannot be calmed. (49:23).
Damascus has become feeble; she has turned to flee. Panic has gripped her; anguish and pain have seized her like a woman in labor. (49:24).
How is the city of praise not forsaken, the town that brings Me joy? (49:25).
For her young men will fall in the streets, and all her warriors will be silenced in that day,” declares the LORD of Hosts. (49:26).
“I will set fire to the walls of Damascus; it will consume the fortresses of Ben-hadad.” (49:27).
Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated, this is what the LORD says: “Rise up, advance against Kedar, and destroy the people of the east! (49:28).
They will take their tents and flocks, their tent curtains and all their goods. They will take their camels for themselves. They will shout to them: ‘Terror is on every side!’ (49:29).
Run! Escape quickly! Lie low, O residents of Hazor,” declares the LORD, “for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has drawn up a plan against you; he has devised a strategy against you. (49:30).
Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, one that dwells securely,” declares the LORD. “They have no gates or bars; they live alone. (49:31).

Their camels will become plunder, and their large herds will be spoil. I will scatter to the wind in every direction those who shave their temples; I will bring calamity on them from all sides,” declares the LORD. (49:32).
“Hazor will become a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever. No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” (49:33).
This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. (49:34).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Behold, I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might. (49:35).
I will bring the four winds against Elam from the four corners of the heavens, and I will scatter them to all these winds. There will not be a nation to which Elam’s exiles will not go. (49:36).

So I will shatter Elam before their foes, before those who seek their lives. I will bring disaster upon them, even My fierce anger,” declares the LORD. “I will send out the sword after them until I finish them off. (49:37).
I will set My throne in Elam, and destroy its king and officials,” declares the LORD. (49:38).
“Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity,” declares the LORD. (49:39).
crossRefs: Obadiah 1:1-14: Edom's pride in the clefts of the rock and its violence against Jacob, at chapter length.
Amos 1:11-15: Oracles against Edom for pursuing his brother with the sword, and against Ammon.
Genesis 36:9-11: Teman named in Esau's line, the Edomite district whose famed wisdom, this chapter says, will not save it.
Deuteronomy 2:19: Ammon's land given to the descendants of Lot and closed to Israel, the inheritance 49:1 says was seized.
Genesis 25:23-26: Jacob and Esau in the womb, the origin of the grudge that runs through every Edom oracle.

stories.title: 🧱 Jeremiah 50
summaryBullets: This is the word that the LORD spoke through Jeremiah the prophet concerning Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans: (50:1).

“Announce and declare to the nations; lift up a banner and proclaim it; hold nothing back when you say, ‘Babylon is captured; Bel is put to shame; Marduk is shattered, her images are disgraced, her idols are broken in pieces.’ (50:2).
For a nation from the north will come against her; it will make her land a desolation. No one will live in it; both man and beast will flee.” (50:3).
“In those days and at that time, declares the LORD, the children of Israel and the children of Judah will come together, weeping as they come, and will seek the LORD their God. (50:4).
They will ask the way to Zion and turn their faces toward it. They will come and join themselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten. (50:5).
My people are lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray, causing them to roam the mountains. They have wandered from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place. (50:6).
All who found them devoured them, and their enemies said, ‘We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their true pasture, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.’ (50:7).
Flee from the midst of Babylon; depart from the land of the Chaldeans; be like the he-goats that lead the flock. (50:8).

For behold, I stir up and bring against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the land of the north. They will line up against her; from the north she will be captured. Their arrows will be like skilled warriors who do not return empty-handed. (50:9).
Chaldea will be plundered; all who plunder her will have their fill,” declares the LORD. (50:10).
“Because you rejoice, because you sing in triumph— you who plunder My inheritance— because you frolic like a heifer treading grain and neigh like stallions, (50:11).
your mother will be greatly ashamed; she who bore you will be disgraced. Behold, she will be the least of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. (50:12).
Because of the wrath of the LORD, she will not be inhabited; she will become completely desolate. All who pass through Babylon will be horrified and will hiss at all her wounds. (50:13).
Line up in formation around Babylon, all you who draw the bow! Shoot at her! Spare no arrows! For she has sinned against the LORD. (50:14).

Raise a war cry against her on every side! She has thrown up her hands in surrender; her towers have fallen; her walls are torn down. Since this is the vengeance of the LORD, take out your vengeance upon her; as she has done, do the same to her. (50:15).
Cut off the sower from Babylon, and the one who wields the sickle at harvest time. In the face of the oppressor’s sword, each will turn to his own people, each will flee to his own land. (50:16).
Israel is a scattered flock, chased away by lions. The first to devour him was the king of Assyria; the last to crush his bones was Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.” (50:17).
Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “I will punish the king of Babylon and his land as I punished the king of Assyria. (50:18).
I will return Israel to his pasture, and he will graze on Carmel and Bashan; his soul will be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and Gilead. (50:19).

In those days and at that time, declares the LORD, a search will be made for Israel’s guilt, but there will be none, and for Judah’s sins, but they will not be found; for I will forgive the remnant I preserve. (50:20).
Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the residents of Pekod. Kill them and devote them to destruction. Do all that I have commanded you,” declares the LORD. (50:21).
“The noise of battle is in the land — the noise of great destruction. (50:22).
How the hammer of the whole earth lies broken and shattered! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations! (50:23).
I laid a snare for you, O Babylon, and you were caught before you knew it. You were found and captured because you challenged the LORD. (50:24).
The LORD has opened His armory and brought out His weapons of wrath, for this is the work of the Lord GOD of Hosts in the land of the Chaldeans. (50:25).
Come against her from the farthest border. Break open her granaries; pile her up like mounds of grain. Devote her to destruction; leave her no survivors. (50:26).
Kill all her young bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come — the time of their punishment. (50:27).
Listen to the fugitives and refugees from the land of Babylon, declaring in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple. (50:28).

Summon the archers against Babylon, all who string the bow. Encamp all around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done. For she has defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. (50:29).
Therefore, her young men will fall in the streets, and all her warriors will be silenced in that day,” declares the LORD. (50:30).
“Behold, I am against you, O arrogant one,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts, “for your day has come, the time when I will punish you. (50:31).
The arrogant one will stumble and fall with no one to pick him up. And I will kindle a fire in his cities to consume all those around him.” (50:32).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “The sons of Israel are oppressed, and the sons of Judah as well. All their captors hold them fast, refusing to release them. (50:33).
Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name. He will fervently plead their case so that He may bring rest to the earth, but turmoil to those who live in Babylon. (50:34).
A sword is against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, against those who live in Babylon, and against her officials and wise men. (50:35).
A sword is against her false prophets, and they will become fools. A sword is against her warriors, and they will be filled with terror. (50:36).
A sword is against her horses and chariots and against all the foreigners in her midst, and they will become like women. A sword is against her treasuries, and they will be plundered. (50:37).
A drought is upon her waters, and they will be dried up. For it is a land of graven images, and the people go mad over idols. (50:38).
So the desert creatures and hyenas will live there and ostriches will dwell there. It will never again be inhabited or lived in from generation to generation. (50:39).
As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah along with their neighbors,” declares the LORD, “no one will dwell there; no man will abide there. (50:40).
Behold, an army is coming from the north; a great nation and many kings are stirred up from the ends of the earth. (50:41).
They grasp the bow and spear; they are cruel and merciless. Their voice roars like the sea, and they ride upon horses, lined up like men in formation against you, O Daughter of Babylon. (50:42).
The king of Babylon has heard the report, and his hands hang limp. Anguish has gripped him, pain like that of a woman in labor. (50:43).

Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture. For in an instant I will chase Babylon from her land. Who is the chosen one I will appoint for this? For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” (50:44).

Therefore hear the plans that the LORD has drawn up against Babylon and the strategies He has devised against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away; certainly their pasture will be made desolate because of them. (50:45).
At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will quake; a cry will be heard among the nations. (50:46).
crossRefs: Isaiah 13:17-22: The Medes stirred up against Babylon, and the city left as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
Isaiah 46:1-2: Bel bows down and Nebo stoops, and their images are loaded onto pack animals and carried away.
Daniel 5:30-31: Belshazzar is killed that same night and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.
Ezra 1:1-4: Cyrus proclaims the return, the road home that 50:4-5 describes the people taking.
Revelation 18:4: Come out of her, My people, the same call given in 50:8 and 51:6.

translationNotes.note: Two names for Babylon's chief god. Bel means lord, the same word as the Canaanite Baal; Marduk, spelled Merodach in Hebrew, was the city god of Babylon who headed the pantheon after the empire rose. His image was carried in procession along the great processional way at the new year festival, and a king's right to rule was confirmed by taking that statue's hand. Verse 2 announces that both names are disgraced together.

Verses 17-18 give the whole history of the exile in one sentence: first the king of Assyria devoured Israel, then the king of Babylon broke his bones. Assyria took the northern kingdom in 722 BC; Babylon took Judah in 586 BC. Verse 18 says God will punish the second king as He punished the first, which had already happened when Nineveh fell in 612 BC.

Two real districts of southern Babylonia named in Assyrian records, used in 50:21 because the names double as Hebrew words. Merathaim reads as double rebellion or double bitterness, and Pekod reads as punishment. The oracle picks the two places on the map whose names already say what is about to be done to them.

A technical term for handing something over to God so that it may not be taken as plunder or profited from. It is used of Jericho in Joshua 6:17-19 and of Amalek in 1 Samuel 15:3. In 50:21 and 50:26 it means the sack of Babylon is not a raid for loot; the spoil is forfeit.

translationNotes.term: Like the he-goats before the flock
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 tells the exiles to get out ahead of the fall, and picks a shepherd's image for it. Male goats walked at the head of a mixed flock and the sheep followed them. Verse 8 is telling the Judeans in Babylon to be the first ones moving, not the last.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD proclaims through Jeremiah that Babylon will be captured and destroyed by a northern alliance, while Israel and Judah will return to seek God and receive forgiveness. Babylon's idols, warriors, and treasures will fall to the sword; the land will become desolate like Sodom and Gomorrah.

stories.title: 🧱 Jeremiah 51
summaryBullets: This is what the LORD says: “Behold, I will stir up against Babylon and against the people of Leb-kamai the spirit of a destroyer. (51:1).
I will send strangers to Babylon to winnow her and empty her land; for they will come against her from every side in her day of disaster. (51:2).
Do not let the archer bend his bow or put on his armor. Do not spare her young men; devote all her army to destruction! (51:3).
And they will fall slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and pierced through in her streets. (51:4).
For Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, the LORD of Hosts, though their land is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel.” (51:5).
Flee from Babylon! Escape with your lives! Do not be destroyed in her punishment. For this is the time of the LORD’s vengeance; He will pay her what she deserves. (51:6).
Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk. The nations drank her wine; therefore the nations have gone mad. (51:7).
Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been shattered. Wail for her; get her balm for her pain; perhaps she can be healed. (51:8).
“We tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed. Abandon her! Let each of us go to his own land, for her judgment extends to the sky and reaches to the clouds.” (51:9).
“The LORD has brought forth our vindication; come, let us tell in Zion what the LORD our God has accomplished.” (51:10).

Sharpen the arrows! Fill the quivers! The LORD has aroused the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her, for it is the vengeance of the LORD — vengeance for His temple. (51:11).

Raise a banner against the walls of Babylon; post the guard; station the watchmen; prepare the ambush. For the LORD has both devised and accomplished what He spoke against the people of Babylon. (51:12).
You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut. (51:13).
The LORD of Hosts has sworn by Himself: “Surely I will fill you up with men as with locusts, and they will shout in triumph over you.” (51:14).
The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom and stretched out the heavens by His understanding. (51:15).

When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar; He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses. (51:16).
Every man is senseless and devoid of knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols. For his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them. (51:17).
They are worthless, a work to be mocked. In the time of their punishment they will perish. (51:18).
The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things, and of the tribe of His inheritance — the LORD of Hosts is His name. (51:19).
“You are My war club, My weapon for battle. With you I shatter nations; with you I bring kingdoms to ruin. (51:20).
With you I shatter the horse and rider; with you I shatter the chariot and driver. (51:21).
With you I shatter man and woman; with you I shatter the old man and the youth; with you I shatter the young man and the maiden. (51:22).
With you I shatter the shepherd and his flock; with you I shatter the farmer and his oxen; with you I shatter the governors and officials. (51:23).
Before your very eyes I will repay Babylon and all the dwellers of Chaldea for all the evil they have done in Zion,” declares the LORD. (51:24).

“Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, you who devastate the whole earth, declares the LORD. I will stretch out My hand against you; I will roll you over the cliffs and turn you into a charred mountain. (51:25).
No one shall retrieve from you a cornerstone or a foundation stone, because you will become desolate forever,” declares the LORD. (51:26).

“Raise a banner in the land! Blow the ram’s horn among the nations! Prepare the nations against her. Summon the kingdoms against her — Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. Appoint a captain against her; bring up horses like swarming locusts. (51:27).
Prepare the nations for battle against her — the kings of the Medes, their governors and all their officials, and all the lands they rule. (51:28).
The earth quakes and writhes because the LORD’s intentions against Babylon stand: to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant. (51:29).

The warriors of Babylon have stopped fighting; they sit in their strongholds. Their strength is exhausted; they have become like women. Babylon’s homes have been set ablaze, the bars of her gates are broken. (51:30).
One courier races to meet another, and messenger follows messenger, to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end. (51:31).
The fords have been seized, the marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.” (51:32).

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “The Daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time it is trampled. In just a little while her harvest time will come.” (51:33).

“Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me. He has set me aside like an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he filled his belly with my delicacies and vomited me out. (51:34).
May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon,” says the dweller of Zion. “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea,” says Jerusalem. (51:35).
Therefore this is what the LORD says: “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf; I will dry up her sea and make her springs run dry. (51:36).
Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals, an object of horror and scorn, without inhabitant. (51:37).
They will roar together like young lions; they will growl like lion cubs. (51:38).
While they are flushed with heat, I will serve them a feast, and I will make them drunk so that they may revel; then they will fall asleep forever and never wake up, declares the LORD. (51:39).
I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with male goats. (51:40).
How Sheshach has been captured! The praise of all the earth has been seized. What a horror Babylon has become among the nations! (51:41).
The sea has come up over Babylon; she is covered in turbulent waves. (51:42).
Her cities have become a desolation, a dry and arid land, a land where no one lives, where no son of man passes through. (51:43).
I will punish Bel in Babylon. I will make him spew out what he swallowed. The nations will no longer stream to him; even the wall of Babylon will fall. (51:44).
Come out of her, My people! Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD. (51:45).

Do not let your heart grow faint, and do not be afraid when the rumor is heard in the land; for a rumor will come one year— and then another the next year— of violence in the land and of ruler against ruler. (51:46).
Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the idols of Babylon. Her entire land will suffer shame, and all her slain will lie fallen within her. (51:47).
Then heaven and earth and all that is in them will shout for joy over Babylon because the destroyers from the north will come against her,” declares the LORD. (51:48).
“Babylon must fall on account of the slain of Israel, just as the slain of all the earth have fallen because of Babylon. (51:49).
You who have escaped the sword, depart and do not linger! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind.” (51:50).
“We are ashamed because we have heard reproach; disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD’s house.” (51:51).
“Therefore, behold, the days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when I will punish her idols, and throughout her land the wounded will groan. (51:52).
Even if Babylon ascends to the heavens and fortifies her lofty stronghold, the destroyers I send will come against her,” declares the LORD. (51:53).
“The sound of a cry comes from Babylon, the sound of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! (51:54).
For the LORD will destroy Babylon; He will silence her mighty voice. The waves will roar like great waters; the tumult of their voices will resound. (51:55).
For a destroyer is coming against her — against Babylon. Her warriors will be captured, and their bows will be broken, for the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full. (51:56).

I will make her princes and wise men drunk, along with her governors, officials, and warriors. Then they will fall asleep forever and not wake up,” declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts. (51:57).

This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Babylon’s thick walls will be leveled, and her high gates consumed by fire. So the labor of the people will be for nothing; the nations will exhaust themselves to fuel the flames.” (51:58).

This is the message that Jeremiah the prophet gave to the quartermaster Seraiah son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, when he went to Babylon with King Zedekiah of Judah in the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign. (51:59).
Jeremiah had written on a single scroll about all the disaster that would come upon Babylon — all these words that had been written concerning Babylon. (51:60).
And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, “When you get to Babylon, see that you read all these words aloud, (51:61).
and say, ‘O LORD, You have promised to cut off this place so that no one will remain — neither man nor beast. Indeed, it will be desolate forever.’ (51:62).
When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates. (51:63).
Then you are to say, ‘In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again, because of the disaster I will bring upon her. And her people will grow weary.’” Here end the words of Jeremiah. (51:64).
crossRefs: Isaiah 44:28-45:3: Cyrus named beforehand, with the rivers dried up and the two-leaved gates opened before him.
Daniel 5:1-6: Belshazzar drinks from the vessels taken out of the temple in Jerusalem, on the night the city fell.
Revelation 18:21: A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, the same sign as the stone tied to the scroll in 51:63.
Genesis 11:1-9: Babel, the tower, and the confusing of speech, where the name of this city first appears.
Psalm 137:8-9: The exiles by Babylon's rivers pronounce repayment on the city for what it did to them.

translationNotes.term: A scroll sunk in the Euphrates
translationNotes.note: Verses 59-64 record a sign act carried out nine hundred miles from home. Seraiah, Baruch's brother, travels to Babylon on state business in Zedekiah's fourth year, about 594 BC, carrying a scroll of these words. He is told to read the whole thing aloud there, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, then say: so Babylon will sink and not rise. The book's last recorded act by Jeremiah is a document deliberately destroyed, and a copy of it survives as the chapter you are reading.

Literally the officer of the resting place, the official who arranged a royal party's overnight stops, quarters and supplies on the road. Verse 59 gives Seraiah that post on Zedekiah's journey to Babylon, which is exactly the job that would let a man carry a private scroll into the capital and get an hour alone at the river.

Three peoples summoned against Babylon in 51:27, all from the mountains north of Mesopotamia. Ararat is Urartu in Assyrian records, around Lake Van in eastern Anatolia; Minni is the Mannaeans, their neighbours to the southeast; Ashkenaz is the Scythians. The call is for hill peoples who fielded cavalry and archers, and 51:11 and 51:28 name the Medes commanding them.

Verse 58 says the broad walls of Babylon will be levelled and her high gates set on fire. Babylon's defences were real and famous: a double wall of mud brick wide enough to drive on, ringed by a moat fed from the Euphrates, with monumental gateways including the Ishtar Gate faced in glazed blue brick. Verse 53 concedes the point in advance, saying that even if she fortified her lofty stronghold, destroyers would still come.

Verse 25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain and says it will be rolled down from the crags and left as a burnt mountain, with 51:26 adding that no one will take a cornerstone or a foundation stone from her. Reusing dressed stone from a ruin was normal practice everywhere in the ancient world. The point is that the rubble will not even be worth quarrying.

Verses 32 and 36 speak of the river crossings seized and the sea and springs of Babylon dried up. The city straddled the Euphrates and drew its moat and its water supply from it. Isaiah 44:27 uses the same image of Cyrus, and the drying of the channel is the way the classical historians describe the Persian entry.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD declares he will destroy Babylon through invading forces because it has oppressed Israel and Judah; he commands the people to flee the city and instructs Jeremiah to have Seraiah read a written prophecy of Babylon's destruction aloud there and sink it in the Euphrates as a sign.

headings.text: Praise to the God of Jacob

stories.title: 🏚️ Jeremiah 52
summaryBullets: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah; she was from Libnah. (52:1).
And Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done. (52:2).
For because of the anger of the LORD, all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until He finally banished them from His presence. And Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon. (52:3).

So in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it. (52:4).
And the city was kept under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year. (52:5).
By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food. (52:6).

Then the city was breached; and though the Chaldeans had surrounded the city, all the men of war fled the city by night by way of the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden. They headed toward the Arabah, (52:7).
but the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army deserted him. (52:8).
The Chaldeans seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where he pronounced judgment on Zedekiah. (52:9).
There at Riblah the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and he also killed all the officials of Judah. (52:10).
Then he put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon, where he kept him in custody until his dying day. (52:11).
On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign over Babylon, Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. (52:12).
He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem — every significant building. (52:13).
And the whole army of the Chaldeans under the captain of the guard broke down all the walls around Jerusalem. (52:14).

Then Nebuzaradan captain of the guard carried into exile some of the poorest people and those who remained in the city, along with the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon and the rest of the craftsmen. (52:15).
But Nebuzaradan captain of the guard left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields. (52:16).
Moreover, the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD, and they carried all the bronze to Babylon. (52:17).
They also took away the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and all the articles of bronze used in the temple service. (52:18).
The captain of the guard also took away the basins, censers, sprinkling bowls, pots, lampstands, pans, and drink offering bowls— anything made of pure gold or fine silver. (52:19).

As for the two pillars, the Sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it, and the movable stands that King Solomon had made for the house of the LORD, the weight of the bronze from all these articles was beyond measure. (52:20).
Each pillar was eighteen cubits tall and twelve cubits in circumference; each was hollow, four fingers thick. (52:21).
The bronze capital atop one pillar was five cubits high, with a network of bronze pomegranates all around. The second pillar, with its pomegranates, was similar. (52:22).
Each capital had ninety-six pomegranates on the sides, and a total of a hundred pomegranates were above the surrounding network. (52:23).
The captain of the guard also took away Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest of second rank, and the three doorkeepers. (52:24).

Of those still in the city, he took a court official who had been appointed over the men of war, as well as seven trusted royal advisers. He also took the scribe of the captain of the army, who had enlisted the people of the land, and sixty men who were found in the city. (52:25).
Nebuzaradan captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. (52:26).
There at Riblah in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death. So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land. (52:27).
These are the people Nebuchadnezzar carried away: in the seventh year, 3,023 Jews; (52:28).
in Nebuchadnezzar’s eighteenth year, 832 people from Jerusalem; (52:29).
in Nebuchadnezzar’s twenty-third year, Nebuzaradan captain of the guard carried away 745 Jews. So in all, 4,600 people were taken away. (52:30).

On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the first year of the reign of Evil-merodach king of Babylon, he pardoned Jehoiachin king of Judah and released him from prison. (52:31).
And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. (52:32).
So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life. (52:33).
And the king of Babylon provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life, until the day of his death. (52:34).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 24:18-25:30: The parallel account of the last king, the fall, the exile and Jehoiachin's release.
Jeremiah 39:1-10: The book's earlier and shorter account of the same siege and breach.
1 Kings 7:15-26: Solomon makes the two bronze pillars and the bronze Sea that 52:17-23 measures as plunder.
Ezra 1:7-11: Cyrus counts the temple vessels back out of the treasury and returns them to Judah.
2 Chronicles 36:17-21: The same fall told with the land keeping its sabbaths for seventy years.

translationNotes.note: Verses 28-30 give a scribe's tally in three lines: 3,023 Judeans in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 832 from Jerusalem in his eighteenth, and 745 taken by Nebuzaradan in his twenty-third, for a stated total of 4,600. These are far smaller than the figures in 2 Kings 24:14-16, which counts ten thousand and then seven thousand plus a thousand craftsmen. The lists are counting different things; a register of adult men is not a count of households, and the third deportation in the twenty-third year appears nowhere else.

Verses 21-22 measure them: eighteen cubits tall, about twenty-seven feet (8 m), twelve cubits around, hollow, with walls four fingers thick and a bronze capital five cubits high on top wreathed in pomegranates. 1 Kings 7:15-22 records that Solomon set them at the temple porch and named them Jachin and Boaz. Verse 17 says the Chaldeans broke them up on site, because you cannot move eight metres of cast bronze whole.

A cast bronze basin standing on twelve bronze bulls in the temple court, used by the priests for washing. 1 Kings 7:23-26 gives it as ten cubits across, thirty around and five deep, holding two thousand baths, roughly eleven thousand gallons (44,000 litres). Verse 20 says the weight of bronze in the pillars, the Sea and the stands was beyond measure, and all of it went to Babylon as metal.

Verses 24-27 list who was taken north to Nebuchadnezzar's field headquarters and put to death there: the chief priest Seraiah, the second priest Zephaniah, three doorkeepers, the officer over the fighting men, seven royal advisers, the army recruiting scribe, and sixty men of the land. That is the leadership of the temple, the army and the civil service, executed together. Riblah on the Orontes lay about two hundred miles (320 km) north of Jerusalem.

The Babylonian king Awil-Marduk, son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned from 562 to 560 BC. Verses 31-34 record that in his accession year he released Jehoiachin from prison after thirty-seven years, gave him a seat above the other captive kings, and put him on a daily allowance for life. Ration tablets excavated in Babylon list oil issued to Yaukin king of the land of Yahud and to his sons, which is this man by name.

translationNotes.term: A different day for the burning
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 dates the burning of the temple to the tenth day of the fifth month; 2 Kings 25:8 gives the seventh day of the same month. Both accounts place it in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. The two records report different days within the same operation, and neither is a summary of the other; chapter 52 carries details Kings lacks, including the deportation tally in 52:28-30.

stories.keyTakeaway: The appendix restates the fall, exile, and temple loss with numbers and vessel lists, then ends with Jehoiachin’s release and regular provision in Babylon.

intro:
Jeremiah was written by Jeremiah son of Hilkiah (Jeremiah 1:1), the priest from Anathoth, with his scribe Baruch son of Neriah recording many of the oracles by dictation (Jeremiah 36:4, 32; 45:1). The book was composed over Jeremiah's prophetic ministry of roughly forty-six years, from 627 BC to about 580 BC. Jeremiah was born around 645 BC in Anathoth, a Levitical town three miles north of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, the son of Hilkiah the priest, of the line of Abiathar (the priest whom Solomon had exiled to Anathoth in 1 Kings 2:26-27). He was called to prophesy in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (627 BC), still a young man of around eighteen to twenty years, and ministered through the reigns of Judah's last five kings: Josiah (640-609 BC), Jehoahaz (609 BC, three months), Jehoiakim (609-598 BC), Jehoiachin (598 BC, three months), and Zedekiah (597-586 BC). He was forbidden by God to marry (Jeremiah 16:1-2), was repeatedly persecuted by court officials and religious leaders, was thrown into a muddy cistern and left to die (rescued by an Ethiopian court official named Ebed-Melech, Jeremiah 38), and watched the city of Jerusalem fall to Nebuchadnezzar II's armies in 586 BC. After the fall, a remnant of Judahites taking refuge from Babylonian reprisals forced Jeremiah against his will to accompany them into Egypt, where tradition holds he was eventually stoned to death by his own people. Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's faithful scribe and friend, recorded the prophecies in scrolls; an archaeological seal impression bearing the inscription "Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe" has been recovered from the period, corresponding to the biblical Baruch. The same Jeremiah who also wrote Lamentations and who is credited by Jewish tradition (Talmud Baba Bathra 15a) with composing 1 and 2 Kings during his exile in Egypt.

The historical setting is the collapse of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and the rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire over the ancient Near East. When Jeremiah began his ministry in 627 BC, Assyria under Ashurbanipal still dominated the region; within fifteen years Assyria had collapsed. Nineveh fell to a Babylonian-Median coalition in 612 BC, and Nabopolassar of Babylon defeated the Egyptians under Pharaoh Necho II at the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BC, transferring Near Eastern hegemony to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar II succeeded Nabopolassar that year and conducted three deportations of Judah: 605 BC (Daniel and the young nobles), 597 BC (King Jehoiachin, Ezekiel, and ten thousand exiles), and 586 BC (the destruction of Jerusalem and Solomon's temple, the final deportation, and the end of the Davidic kingdom). Egypt under the 26th Dynasty (the Saite Period) and its Pharaoh Necho II briefly held the Levant after Assyria's collapse but lost it to Babylon at Carchemish. Greece was in the late Archaic period; Solon was reforming the laws of Athens, and the earliest Greek philosophers (Thales of Miletus and the other Pre-Socratics) were just beginning to write.

Jeremiah is the twenty-fourth book of the Christian Old Testament and the second of the four Major Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel). The Hebrew name Yirmeyahu (יִרְמְיָהוּ) means "Yahuah will lift up" or "Yahuah establishes," combining a verbal root with the divine name Yah. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Jeremiah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with several scrolls (4QJer-a, 4QJer-b, 4QJer-c, 4QJer-d) dating from the 3rd century BC through the 1st century AD; some of these Qumran copies preserve a shorter Hebrew text close to the Greek Septuagint version, while others preserve the longer Masoretic version, indicating that two ancient Hebrew text-forms of Jeremiah circulated side by side in the late Second Temple period.
